Wealthy
[COLOR_POSITIVE_TEXT]Wealthy[ENDCOLOR] City-States are prosperous and generous to new friends, but less swayed by gold gifts. Trade routes to them yield more gold, and it is easier to demand tribute from.
Impoverished
[COLOR_POSITIVE_TEXT]Impoverished[ENDCOLOR] City-States struggle financially. They give less gold on first contact, but respond more strongly to gold gifts and may ask for gold even when they have not been bullied.
Pirate Republic
[COLOR_POSITIVE_TEXT]Pirate Republic[ENDCOLOR] City-States are coastal militaristic enclaves ruled by privateers. They favor aggressive quests and may gift naval units to allies with ocean access.
Theocratic
[COLOR_POSITIVE_TEXT]Theocratic[ENDCOLOR] City-States let religion dominate their diplomacy. Shared faith strengthens influence ties; different faiths weaken them. The first player to spread a religion here receives a burst of influence.
Pacifistic
[COLOR_POSITIVE_TEXT]Pacifistic[ENDCOLOR] City-States avoid war and military buildup. They never join allies in war, but refuse gifts from civilizations at war with their ally. They pay more when bullied for gold.
Isolationist
[COLOR_POSITIVE_TEXT]Isolationist[ENDCOLOR] City-States keep to themselves. They offer no quests and accept no gifts. Declaring war on an Isolationist City-State does not anger other City-States or forfeit Friendly City-State bonuses. Once any civilization reaches the Modern Era, they adopt a new random personality.
Influence with a befriended [COLOR_POSITIVE_TEXT]Friendly[ENDCOLOR] City-State decays more slowly, and completing quests grants +25% more influence. These bonuses are lost if you have ever declared war on a City-State (except Isolationist City-States).

O great Mansa Musa, Lion of Mali and lord of the golden lands, your people look to you beneath the burning sun of the Sahel. From the banks of the Niger to the sands of the Sahara, merchants speak your name with awe, for the caravans of gold, salt, ivory, and learning flow through your empire like lifeblood through the veins of the world.[NEWLINE][NEWLINE]You inherit a realm already rich in earth and trade, yet it is by wisdom, faith, and command that riches become greatness. Mansa Musa
[COLOR_XP_BLUE]https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mansa_Musa[ENDCOLOR][NEWLINE][NEWLINE]Mansa Musa[b] (c.1280 - c.1337) was the ninth Mansa of the Mali Empire, which reached its territorial peak during his reign. Musa's reign is often regarded as the zenith of Mali's power and prestige, although he features less in Mandinka oral traditions than his predecessors. Musa went on Hajj to Mecca in 1324, traveling with an enormous entourage and a vast supply of gold. En route he spent time in Cairo, where his lavish gift-giving is said to have noticeably affected the value of gold in Egypt and garnered the attention of the wider Muslim world. Musa expanded the borders of the Mali Empire, in particular incorporating the cities of Gao and Timbuktu into its territory. He sought closer ties with the rest of the Muslim world, particularly the Mamluk and Marinid Sultanates. He recruited scholars from the wider Muslim world to travel to Mali, such as the Andalusian poet Abu Ishaq al-Sahili, and helped establish Timbuktu as a center of Islamic learning. His reign is associated with numerous construction projects, including a portion of Djinguereber Mosque in Timbuktu.
Grand Treasury of Mali[COLOR_CULTURE_STORED]*[ENDCOLOR]
[COLOR_XP_BLUE]https://www.worldhistory.org/Mali_Empire/[ENDCOLOR][NEWLINE][NEWLINE]The Grand Treasury of Mali represents the imperial wealth of the mansa: gold from Bambuk, Bure, and Galam; salt from Saharan trade; tribute from subject peoples; and taxes from caravans crossing Mali's domains. Though not a single documented building, it reflects the financial power that made Mali one of the richest states of the medieval world and made Mansa Musa's pilgrimage famous from West Africa to Cairo.
The Grand Treasury can be a potent force multiplier with a high [ICON_GOLD] Gold or [ICON_PEACE] Faith income by discounting the first purchase in the city it's made in.
[COLOR_CULTURE_STORED]Unique National Wonder (only [COLOR_GREEN]Mali[ENDCOLOR] may build one)[ENDCOLOR][NEWLINE][NEWLINE]In addition to the effects of the [ICON_WONDER_NATIONAL_TREASURY] [COLOR_YELLOW]East India Company[ENDCOLOR] that it replaces, the Grand Treasury of Mali provides +5 [ICON_PEACE] Faith and a [COLOR_GREEN]25%[ENDCOLOR] discount to the first Unit or Building purchased in the city each Turn with [ICON_GOLD] Gold or [ICON_PEACE] Faith. Requires a [ICON_BUILDING_MARKET] [COLOR_YELLOW]Market[ENDCOLOR] to be constructed, but does not require a [ICON_BUILDING_MARKET] [COLOR_YELLOW]Market[ENDCOLOR] in all cities.

Buganda
Hail Kabaka Muteesa I, guardian of Buganda and lord of the hills above Nnalubaale, your people gather beneath the royal drums. From the shores of the great lake to the roads of the interior, your kingdom stands strong yet beyond your borders, the world presses closer. Traders from the coast bring cloth, guns, and foreign prayers. Missionaries speak of distant kings and new gods. Some arrive with gifts, some with promises, and some with ambitions hidden beneath polite words.[NEWLINE][NEWLINE]Wise Muteesa, you must weigh each stranger as carefully as a spear in the hand. Let no faith, merchant, or empire master Buganda while you still command the court. Take what strengthens your kingdom, reject what would divide it, and make the palace at Mengo a place where foreign powers compete for your favor.[NEWLINE][NEWLINE]O Kabaka, will you guide Buganda through the age of traders, missionaries, and empires? Can you build a civilization that will stand the test of time?
Kabaka Muteesa I
[COLOR_XP_BLUE]https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muteesa_I_of_Buganda [ENDCOLOR][NEWLINE][NEWLINE]Muteesa I Mukaabya Walugembe Kayiira (c. 1837-9 October 1884) was the 30th Kabaka of the Kingdom of Buganda, from 1856 until 1884. In Ugandan historiography, Muteesa left a mixed legacy, with some regarding him as the most important of the kings of Buganda because of his vision and diplomatic skills, while others are more critical and believe he welcomed foreign influence that ultimately undermined Buganda's sovereignty.

[COLOR_XP_BLUE] (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Akkadian_Empire)[ENDCOLOR]The Akkadian Empire (/əˈkeɪdiən/)[2] was the first known empire,[3] succeeding the long-lived city-states of Sumer. Blessings upon you, Vladislav II, wise King of Bohemia and Hungary! Your reign ushered in a golden era of peace and cultural prosperity for the Czech lands. Under your rule, the magnificent Vladislav Hall of Prague Castle was constructed, standing as a testament to your patronage of Gothic architecture and the arts. Though remembered as a peaceful and consensus-seeking monarch, your legacy endures in the grand buildings and institutions that flourished during your reign.[NEWLINE][NEWLINE]Great King, your people call for your leadership once more. Thaler Mint
The Thaler was a silver coin first minted in Jáchymov (then known as Joachimsthal) in the Kingdom of Bohemia in 1520. These coins gained immediate popularity throughout Europe due to their consistent weight and purity, setting a standard that influenced currency systems across the continent and beyond. Indeed, the word "dollar" evolved from "thaler." The Kutná Hora silver mines, among the most productive in medieval Europe, provided material for the Prague Groschen and later thalers, making Bohemia a center of European minting. Czech mints became renowned for their advanced metallurgical techniques and artistic coin designs, contributing significantly to the economic strength of the Bohemian kingdom and later the Habsburg monarchy.
Czech replacement for the [ICON_BUILDING_MINT] Mint. Costs 25% less [ICON_PRODUCTION] Production to construct. Provides +2 [ICON_GOLD] Gold from [ICON_RES_IRON] Iron in addition to standard mint resources. Includes 1 [ICON_GREAT_MERCHANT] Great Merchant [ICON_CITIZEN_GOLD] Specialist slot.
The Thaler Mint is a versatile improvement on the standard Mint, available at the same technology but costing 25% less [ICON_PRODUCTION] Production. Beyond providing the usual bonuses for gold, silver, and copper resources, it also gains bonuses from [ICON_RES_IRON] Iron, making it valuable even in cities without traditional mint resources. The included Merchant specialist slot helps generate additional [ICON_GOLD] Gold and Great Merchant points.

History
Vladislav II Jagiellon (1456-1516), King of Bohemia from 1471 and King of Hungary and Croatia from 1490, was a member of the Jagiellon dynasty who ruled during a significant transitional period in Central European history. Known for his mild temperament and diplomatic acumen, Vladislav ascended to the Bohemian throne after the death of the Hussite king George of Poděbrady, and was selected partly because he promised religious tolerance in a kingdom divided between Catholics and Hussites. His reign in Bohemia was characterized by his efforts to balance royal authority with the growing power of the nobility and urban communities. In 1490, he was elected King of Hungary following the death of Matthias Corvinus, creating a personal union between the two kingdoms. Though sometimes criticized for his perceived weakness in standing up to the nobility (earning him the nickname "King Dobře," or "King All-Right," for his tendency to agree with whatever was proposed), Vladislav was in reality a shrewd ruler who preferred negotiation to confrontation. His architectural legacy includes the magnificent Vladislav Hall in Prague Castle, one of the most spectacular late Gothic spaces in Central Europe. During his reign, Prague experienced significant cultural development, with printing presses established and Renaissance influences beginning to appear alongside Gothic traditions. The legal code he established in 1500, known as the Vladislav Land Ordinance, remained a foundation of Czech law for centuries. While not remembered as a military leader or forceful monarch, Vladislav II's diplomatic approach and cultural patronage made him an important figure in Czech history who maintained peace and prosperity during his 45-year reign.

Blessings upon you, Akbar the Great, wise ruler of the Mughal Empire! Your leadership transformed a realm of disparate peoples into one of history's most powerful and prosperous empires. Your administrative brilliance and religious tolerance fostered an era of unprecedented cultural and artistic achievement. Under your reign, the Mughal Empire expanded across the Indian subcontinent through both conquest and diplomacy. Your Din-i-Ilahi faith and Sulh-i-kul policy of religious harmony helped unite a diverse population, while your patronage of the arts, literature, and architecture left a legacy that still inspires the world today.[NEWLINE][NEWLINE]O great emperor, your people call for your wisdom once more. Can you build an empire that honors diverse faiths and cultures? Can you create a civilization that will stand the test of time?
Mansabdari Estate
The Mansabdari system was a unique administrative structure established by Emperor Akbar that formed the backbone of the Mughal Empire's civil and military administration. Under this system, imperial officers known as mansabdars were assigned ranks (mansabs) that determined their status, responsibilities, and compensation. Each mansabdar maintained estates that served as centers of local governance and military recruitment. These estates not only strengthened imperial control but also served as cultural centers that promoted Mughal artistic and architectural styles. The system helped integrate diverse ethnic and religious groups into the empire's administrative framework, reflecting the Mughals' skill at incorporating various cultural traditions into their governance model.
Mughal replacement for the Caravansary. Available at Currency (vs. Horseback Riding). Provides +10 City [ICON_STRENGTH] Strength, +2 [ICON_GOLD] Gold and +3 [ICON_CULTURE] Culture if the city has a garrison. Provides 2 [ICON_RES_HORSE] Horse resource for the Empire.
The Mansabdari Estate is available at a different technology than the Caravansary it replaces, requiring Currency rather than Horseback Riding. Beyond improving land trade routes, it provides significant defensive bonuses to your cities and additional [ICON_GOLD] Gold and [ICON_CULTURE] Culture when the city is garrisoned, encouraging a balanced approach to growth and defense.

Zafarbaksh
The Zafarbaksh, meaning "victory bestower" in Persian, was an advanced artillery piece developed during the Mughal Empire's military prime. Mughal artillery benefited from a combination of Ottoman, Persian, and indigenous Indian engineering traditions, creating weapons that were both mobile and powerful. While European cannons of the period were often unwieldy in the varied terrain of the subcontinent, Mughal engineers modified their designs with lighter materials and improved carriage systems. Under Emperor Akbar's military reforms, these cannons became a cornerstone of Mughal battlefield supremacy, with specialized crews trained to rapidly deploy and reposition them during battles. The Zafarbaksh cannons were particularly feared for their effective range and mobility, allowing Mughal forces to outmaneuver opponents while maintaining superior firepower. The Mughal's mastery of metallurgy also enabled them to cast more uniform and reliable cannon barrels that could withstand repeated firing.
Mughal replacement for the [ICON_UNIT_CANNON] Cannon. Has a higher [ICON_STRENGTH] Combat Strength (18 vs 14), higher [ICON_RANGE_STRENGTH] Ranged Strength (23 vs 20), improved [ICON_MOVES] Movement (3 vs 2), and has no sight penalty, but is more costly to build.
The Zafarbaksh is a powerful and mobile siege weapon that excels at taking cities. With higher combat and ranged strength than the standard Cannon, plus an extra movement point and no sight penalties, it can position effectively for attacks. While more expensive to produce, its superior mobility and firepower make it a worthy investment for expanding your empire through conquest. Unlike other unique units however, the Zafarbaksh's special abilities do not carry over when it upgrades to Artillery.

Akbar
History
Jalaluddin Muhammad Akbar (1542-1605), known as Akbar the Great, was the third Mughal emperor who ruled from 1556 to 1605. Ascending the throne at just 13 years of age, Akbar transformed the Mughal Empire from a relatively small kingdom into one of the world's greatest powers. His military campaigns expanded Mughal control across most of the Indian subcontinent, but it was his administrative and cultural innovations that truly defined his reign. Akbar's most significant achievement was developing systems of governance that integrated Hindu and Muslim traditions, creating a stable foundation for a diverse empire. His policy of religious tolerance, embodied in his principle of Sulh-i-kul ("peace with all"), was revolutionary for its time. He abolished the jizya tax on non-Muslims, appointed Hindus to high government positions, and even created a syncretic religious movement called Din-i-Ilahi that borrowed elements from various faiths. Under Akbar's patronage, art, architecture, and literature flourished, creating the distinctive Indo-Islamic culture that characterizes the Mughal legacy. The Mansabdari administrative system he developed remained the backbone of Mughal governance for generations. Akbar's pragmatic policies of religious and cultural accommodation established a model of pluralistic rule that would influence Indian governance for centuries.

Ribat
Ribats were fortified Islamic military outposts located along coastal areas to defend against naval attacks. They also served as religious centers and places for spiritual retreat. In Tunisia, ribats played a crucial role in coastal defense against Byzantine naval incursions and later European pirates. The Ribat of Monastir, built in 796 AD, is one of the oldest and most well-preserved examples, combining military defensive structures with religious functions.
Tunisian replacement for the [ICON_BUILDING_CASTLE]Castle. Generates +4 [ICON_GOLDEN_AGE] Golden Age points per turn. Costs 50% less [ICON_PRODUCTION] Production and does not require [ICON_BUILDING_WALLS] Walls.
The Ribat is significantly more accessible than regular Castles since it doesn't require Walls as a prerequisite and costs 50% less [ICON_PRODUCTION] Production. Beyond its defensive capabilities, it generates valuable [ICON_GOLD] Gold and [ICON_PEACE] Faith, while the +4 [ICON_GOLDEN_AGE] Golden Age points per turn help Tunisia trigger Golden Ages more frequently.

Xebec
The Xebec was a Mediterranean sailing ship with a distinctive hull and complex sail arrangement that made it both fast and maneuverable. It was the preferred vessel of the Barbary corsairs who operated from North Africa, including Tunisia. Tunisian corsairs used these specialized vessels to become a formidable naval power in the Mediterranean from the 16th to 19th centuries. The Xebec's shallow draft allowed it to navigate coastal waters while evading larger warships, and its speed made it perfect for capturing merchant vessels. With a combination of lateen and square sails, it could sail closer to the wind than square-rigged vessels. The Tunisian Xebecs, commanded by corsairs like Dragut and Uluj Ali, were particularly feared for their raids on European shipping and coastal settlements from Italy to Iceland.
Tunisian replacement for the [ICON_UNIT_PRIVATEER] Privateer. Has a higher [ICON_STRENGTH] Combat Strength, may capture [COLOR_POSITIVE_TEXT]Enemy[ENDCOLOR] ships (50% chance), and spends no [ICON_MOVES] movement pilaging tiles. Is more expensive to build.
The Xebec is Tunisia's unique naval unit, replacing the Privateer. With higher combat strength and the ability to capture defeated enemy ships, the Xebec allows you to quickly build a powerful fleet. Use them to raid coastal routes and cities, as they can pillage without spending movement points. While they cost more than standard Privateers, their advantages in combat and mobility make them worthwhile investments for a naval power.

Farhat Hached
History
Farhat Hached (1914-1952) was a prominent Tunisian labor leader and national independence activist. Born to a modest family in coastal Tunisia, he began working at a young age and quickly became involved in labor organizing. In 1946, he founded the powerful Tunisian General Labour Union (UGTT), which became crucial in Tunisia's independence movement. Hached transformed labor activism into a nationalist struggle, working alongside political leaders like Habib Bourguiba. His growing influence made him a target, and he was assassinated in 1952, likely by French colonial agents. His martyrdom galvanized the independence movement, and Tunisia gained independence four years after his death. Hached remains a national hero, remembered for his commitment to workers' rights and national sovereignty.

Arsenal of Venice
[COLOR_POSITIVE_TEXT]Naval Units[ENDCOLOR] cost 33% more [ICON_PRODUCTION] Production. Produces 1 extra copy of every [COLOR_POSITIVE_TEXT]Naval Unit[ENDCOLOR] built in the city using [ICON_PRODUCTION] Production.[NEWLINE][NEWLINE]City must be built on the coast.
The Arsenal of Venice (Italian: Arsenale di Venezia) was one of the most important naval complexes in European history, serving as the heart of Venice's maritime empire from the 12th to 18th centuries. Located in the Castello district of Venice, this vast shipyard complex revolutionized naval construction and became a symbol of Venetian industrial might.[NEWLINE][NEWLINE]At its peak during the Renaissance, the Arsenal employed over 16,000 workers and could produce a complete warship in a single day using revolutionary assembly-line techniques that would later inspire modern industrial production. The complex covered about 15% of Venice's total area and was protected by high walls and fortifications, making it both a center of production and a fortress.[NEWLINE][NEWLINE]The Arsenal's innovative production methods included standardized parts, specialized workers, and efficient logistics systems. Different areas of the complex were dedicated to specific tasks: rope-making, sail production, cannon casting, and hull construction. Ships would move through the Arsenal along a canal system, with workers adding components at each station.[NEWLINE][NEWLINE]The Arsenal's military and economic importance made it one of the most closely guarded secrets of the Venetian Republic. Foreign visitors were rarely allowed inside, and workers were sworn to secrecy about the techniques employed. This industrial complex enabled Venice to maintain naval supremacy in the Mediterranean for centuries and played a crucial role in the city's transformation from a small trading post to a major European power.[NEWLINE][NEWLINE]Today, parts of the Arsenal house the Venice Biennale art exhibition, while other sections serve as a naval base. The iconic gateway, built in 1460, remains one of Venice's most recognizable landmarks and a testament to the Republic's former glory.
[NEWLINE][TAB][TAB]"As in the arsenal of the Venetians, all winter long a stew of sticky pitch boils up to patch their sick and tattered ships that cannot sail (instead of voyaging, some build new keels, some tow and tar the ribs of hulls worn out by too much journeying; some hammer at the prow, some at the stern, and some make oars, and some braid ropes and cords; one mends the jib, another, the mainsail);"[NEWLINE][TAB][TAB] - Dante Alighieri[NEWLINE][TAB]
Tower of Belém
Cities settled on the same landmass where this Wonder has been built receive +1 [ICON_PRODUCTION] Production and +1 [ICON_GOLD] Gold. Cities settled on different landmasses receive +2 [ICON_GOLDEN_AGE] Golden Age Points.[NEWLINE][NEWLINE]Unlocked with the [COLOR_POSITIVE_TEXT]Exploration Policy Tree[ENDCOLOR].
The Tower of Belém (Portuguese: Torre de Belém) stands as one of Portugal's most iconic monuments, situated at the mouth of the Tagus River in Lisbon. Built between 1514 and 1520 during the reign of Manuel I, the tower was commissioned both as a fortress to guard the city's harbor and as a ceremonial gateway to Lisbon.[NEWLINE][NEWLINE]The tower exemplifies Manueline architecture, a distinctly Portuguese late Gothic style that incorporates maritime elements and discoveries from the Age of Discovery. Its intricate stonework features nautical themes, including twisted rope, armillary spheres, and exotic plants. The structure combines military practicality with artistic beauty, featuring both defensive battlements and ornate decorative elements.[NEWLINE][NEWLINE]Originally built on a small island near the Tagus River's bank, the tower now sits close to the shore due to changes in the river's flow over centuries. Its strategic position allowed it to work in tandem with other fortifications to defend Lisbon's maritime entrance.[NEWLINE][NEWLINE]The Tower of Belém has served various purposes throughout its history - from a fortress and customs house to a lighthouse and political prison. Today, it stands as a UNESCO World Heritage site, symbolizing Portugal's maritime power during the Age of Discovery and the architectural splendor of the Manueline style.
[NEWLINE][TAB][TAB]"From this tower, brave souls departed to discover new worlds, and here they returned with the treasures of distant lands."[NEWLINE][TAB][TAB] - Chronicle of Portuguese Discoveries[NEWLINE][TAB]

Yam Route
Yam (Mongolian: Өртөө, Örtöö, checkpoint) was a postal system or supply point route messenger system extensively used and expanded by Ögedei Khan and also used by subsequent Great Khans and Khans. Relay stations provided food, shelter and spare horses for Mongol army messengers. Ögedei Khan gave special attention to Yam because Mongol armies travelled fast, so their messengers had to be even faster, covering 200–300 kilometres (120–190 mi) per day.[1] The system was used to speed up the process of information and intelligence. The system was preserved in Tsarist Russia after the disintegration of the Golden Horde.

Exploration is the act of searching for the purpose of discovery of information or resources, especially in the context of geography or space, rather than research and development that is usually not centred on earth sciences or astronomy. Exploration occurs in all non-sessile animal species, including humans. In human history, its most dramatic rise was during the Age of Discovery when European explorers sailed and charted much of the rest of the world for a variety of reasons. Since then, major explorations after the Age of Discovery have occurred for reasons mostly aimed at information discovery.
Expeditionary warfare is a military invasion of a foreign territory, especially away from established bases. Expeditionary forces were in part the antecedent of the modern concept of rapid deployment forces. Traditionally, expeditionary forces were essentially self-sustaining with an organic logistics capability and with a full array of supporting arms.
The heavy cruiser was a type of cruiser, a naval warship designed for long range and high speed, armed generally with naval guns of roughly 203 mm (8 inches) in caliber, whose design parameters were dictated by the Washington Naval Treaty of 1922 and the London Naval Treaty of 1930. The heavy cruiser is part of a lineage of ship design from 1915 through the early 1950s, although the term "heavy cruiser" only came into formal use in 1930. The heavy cruiser's immediate precursors were the light cruiser designs of the 1900s and 1910s, rather than the armored cruisers of the years before 1905. When the armored cruiser was supplanted by the battlecruiser, an intermediate ship type between this and the light cruiser was found to be needed—one larger and more powerful than the light cruisers of a potential enemy but not as large and expensive as the battlecruiser so as to be built in sufficient numbers to protect merchant ships and serve in a number of combat theaters.
The dreadnought (alternatively spelled dreadnaught) was the predominant type of battleship in the early 20th century. The first of the kind, the Royal Navy's HMS Dreadnought, had such an impact when launched in 1906 that similar battleships built after her were referred to as "dreadnoughts", and earlier battleships became known as pre-dreadnoughts. Her design had two revolutionary features: an "all-big-gun" armament scheme, with an unprecedented number of heavy-calibre guns, and steam turbine propulsion.[a] As dreadnoughts became a crucial symbol of national power, the arrival of these new warships renewed the naval arms race between the United Kingdom and Germany. Dreadnought races sprang up around the world, including in South America, lasting up to the beginning of World War I. Successive designs increased rapidly in size and made use of improvements in armament, armour and propulsion throughout the dreadnought era. Within five years, new battleships outclassed Dreadnought herself. These more powerful vessels were known as "super-dreadnoughts". Most of the original dreadnoughts were scrapped after the end of World War I under the terms of the Washington Naval Treaty, but many of the newer super-dreadnoughts continued serving throughout World War II.

Yugoslavia
Yugoslav
History
Yugoslavia was a country in Southeast Europe and Central Europe for most of the 20th century. It came into existence after World War I in 1918 under the name of the Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes by the merger of the provisional State of Slovenes, Croats and Serbs (which was formed from territories of the former Austro-Hungarian Empire) with the Kingdom of Serbia, and constituted the first union of the South Slavic people as a sovereign state, following centuries in which the region had been part of the Ottoman Empire and Austria-Hungary. Peter I of Serbia was its first sovereign. The kingdom gained international recognition on 13 July 1922 at the Conference of Ambassadors in Paris. The official name of the state was changed to Kingdom of Yugoslavia on 3 October 1929. [NEWLINE][NEWLINE] Yugoslavia was invaded by the Axis powers on 6 April 1941. In 1943, a Democratic Federal Yugoslavia was proclaimed by the Partisan resistance. In 1944 King Peter II, then living in exile, recognised it as the legitimate government. The monarchy was subsequently abolished in November 1945. Yugoslavia was renamed the Federal People's Republic of Yugoslavia in 1946, when a communist government was established. It acquired the territories of Istria, Rijeka, and Zadar from Italy. Partisan leader Josip Broz Tito ruled the country as president until his death in 1980. In 1963, the country was renamed again, as the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia (SFRY).

The authorities of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia established many World War II memorials during its existence. Several memorial sites were established between 1945 and 1960, though widespread building started after the founding of the Non-Aligned Movement. [NEWLINE][NEWLINE] Yugoslav president Josip Broz Tito commissioned several memorial sites and monuments in the 1960s and 1970s dedicated to World War II battles, and Nazi concentration camp sites. They were designed by notable sculptors, including Dušan Džamonja, Vojin Bakić, Miodrag Živković, Jordan and Iskra Grabul, and architects, including Bogdan Bogdanović and Gradimir Medaković. After Tito's death, a small number were built, and the monuments were popular visitor attractions in the 1980s as patriotic sites, and since the Yugoslav Wars and the dissolution of Yugoslavia, the sites are mostly abandoned.

Switzerland
Swiss
History
The establishment of the Old Swiss Confederacy in the Late Middle Ages resulted from a series of military successes against Austria and Burgundy. Swiss independence from the Holy Roman Empire was formally recognised in the Peace of Westphalia in 1648. The Federal Charter of 1291 is considered the founding document of Switzerland, which is celebrated on Swiss National Day. Since the Reformation of the 16th century, Switzerland has maintained a firm policy of armed neutrality; it has not fought an international war since 1815 and did not join the United Nations until 2002. Nevertheless, it pursues an active foreign policy. It is frequently involved in peace-building processes worldwide. Switzerland is the birthplace of the Red Cross, one of the world's oldest and best known humanitarian organisations. It is a founding member of the European Free Trade Association, but notably not part of the European Union, the European Economic Area or the Eurozone. However, it participates in the Schengen Area and the European Single Market through bilateral treaties. (Wikipedia)
Henri Dufour
History
Guillaume Henri Dufour (15 September 1787 – 14 July 1875) was a Swiss army officer, structural engineer and topographer. He served under Napoleon I and held the Swiss office of General four times in his career, firstly in 1847 when he led the Swiss Confederation forces to victory against the Sonderbund. In 1864 Dufour presided over the First Geneva Convention which established the International Red Cross. He was founder and president (1838 to 1865) of the Swiss Federal Office of Topography. (Wikipedia)

Swiss mercenaries (Reisläufer) were notable for their service in foreign armies, especially the armies of the Kings of France, throughout the Early Modern period of European history, from the Later Middle Ages into the Age of Enlightenment. Their service as mercenaries was at its peak during the Renaissance, when their proven battlefield capabilities made them sought-after mercenary troops. There followed a period of decline, as technological and organizational advances counteracted the Swiss' advantages. Switzerland's military isolationism largely put an end to organized mercenary activity; the principal remnant of the practice is the Pontifical Swiss Guard at the Vatican. (Wikipedia)

Ski Resort
Tourists are drawn to Switzerland's diverse landscape as well as the available activities, which take advantage of the Alpine climate and landscapes, in particular for skiing and mountaineering. Tourism began in Switzerland with British mountaineers climbing the main peaks of the Bernese Alps in the early 19th century. The Alpine Club in London was founded in 1857. Reconvalescence in the Alpine climate, in particular from tuberculosis, was another important branch of tourism in the 19th and early 20th centuries: for example in Davos, Graubünden. Due to the prominence of the Bernese Alps in British mountaineering, the Bernese Oberland was long especially known as a tourist destination. Meiringen's Reichenbach Falls achieved literary fame as the site of the fictional death of Sir Arthur Conan Doyle's Sherlock Holmes. The first organised tourist holidays to Switzerland were offered during the 19th century by the Thomas Cook and Lunn Travel companies. Tourism in Switzerland had been exclusively for the rich until the 20th century. It started to become more popular and accessible to others from the early 1900s. (Wikipedia)

Palmyra
Palmyrene
History
The Palmyrene Empire was a short-lived breakaway state from the Roman Empire resulting from the Crisis of the Third Century. Named after its capital city, Palmyra, it encompassed the Roman provinces of Syria Palaestina, Arabia Petraea, and Egypt, as well as large parts of Asia Minor. [NEWLINE][NEWLINE] The Palmyrene Empire was ruled by Queen Zenobia, officially as regent for her son Vaballathus, who inherited the throne in 267 at age ten. In 270, Zenobia rapidly conquered most of the Roman east, attempting to maintain relations with Rome as a legitimate power. In 271, she claimed the imperial title for both herself and her son, fighting a short war with the Roman emperor Aurelian, who conquered Palmyra and captured the self-proclaimed Empress. A year later the Palmyrenes rebelled, which led Aurelian to destroy Palmyra. [NEWLINE][NEWLINE] Despite its brief existence, the Palmyrene Empire is remembered for having been ruled by one of the most ambitious and powerful women in late antiquity. It is also hailed in Syria, where it plays an important role as an icon in Syrian nationalism.
Zenobia
History
Septimia Zenobia was a third-century queen of the Palmyrene Empire in Syria. Many legends surround her ancestry; she was probably not a commoner and she married the ruler of the city, Odaenathus. Her husband became king in 260, elevating Palmyra to supreme power in the Near East by defeating the Sassanians and stabilizing the Roman East. After Odaenathus' assassination, Zenobia became the regent of her son Vaballathus and held de facto power throughout his reign. [NEWLINE][NEWLINE] In 270, Zenobia launched an invasion that brought most of the Roman East under her sway and culminated with the annexation of Egypt. By mid-271 her realm extended from Ancyra, central Anatolia, to southern Egypt, although she remained nominally subordinate to Rome. However, in reaction to the campaign of the Roman emperor Aurelian in 272, Zenobia declared her son emperor and assumed the title of empress (declaring Palmyra's secession from Rome). The Romans were victorious after heavy fighting; the queen was besieged in her capital and captured by Aurelian, who exiled her to Rome, where she spent the remainder of her life. [NEWLINE][NEWLINE] Zenobia was a cultured monarch and fostered an intellectual environment in her court, which was open to scholars and philosophers. She was tolerant toward her subjects and protected religious minorities. The queen maintained a stable administration which governed a multicultural multiethnic empire. Zenobia died after 274, and many tales have been recorded about her fate. Her rise and fall have inspired historians, artists and novelists, and she is a patriotic symbol in Syria.

Clibanarii
The Clibanarii or Klibanophoroi were a Sasanian Persian, late Roman and Byzantine military unit of armored heavy cavalry. Similar to the cataphracti, the horsemen themselves and their horses were fully armoured. There are several theories to the origins of this name, one being that the men were literally nicknamed "camp oven-bearers", due to the amount of armour they wore causing them to heat up very quickly in battle, or that the name is derived from Persian word griwbanwar or griva-pana-bara meaning "neck-guard wearer".[1]

Palmyrene Theater
The second-century CE theatre was built in the center of a semicircular colonnaded piazza which opens up to the South Gate of Palmyra.[2] The 82-by-104-metre (269 by 341 ft) piazza was located to the south-west of the main colonnaded street. The unfinished cavea is 92 metres (302 ft) in diameter and consists only of an ima cavea, the lowest section of the cavea, directly surrounding the orchestra.[3] The ima cavea is organized into eleven cunei of twelve rows each[3] and faces north-northeast towards the cardo maximus.[4] The theatre's aditus maximi, its main entrances, are 3.5 metres (11 ft) in width, and lead to a stone-paved orchestra with a diameter of 23.5 metres (77 ft). The orchestra is bounded by a circular wall with a diameter of 20.3 metres (67 ft).[3] [NEWLINE][NEWLINE] The proscenium wall is decorated with ten curved and nine rectangular niches placed alternately.[3] The stage measures 45.5 by 10.5 metres (149 by 34 ft) and is accessed by two staircases.[5] The scaenae frons had five doors:[6] the main entrance, or valve regia, built into a broad curved niche; two guest doors on either side of the valve regia, or valve hospitalis, built into shallow rectangular niches; and two extra doors, at either end of the stage.[5] Emperor Nero is known to have placed his statue in the niche of the regia of the theatre at Palmyra.[7] The columns at the stage are decorated in the Corinthian order.[5] [NEWLINE][NEWLINE] In the 1950s the theatre was cleared from the sand and subsequently underwent restoration works.[8] The theatre hosted folk music performances for the annual Palmyra festival.

The roots of the Georgian people extend deep in history; their cultural heritage is equally ancient and rich. During the medieval period a powerful Georgian kingdom existed, reaching its height between the 10th and 13th centuries. After a long period of Turkish and Persian domination, Georgia was annexed by the Russian Empire in the 19th century. An independent Georgian state existed from 1918 to 1921, when it was incorporated into the Soviet Union. In 1936 Georgia became a constituent (union) republic and continued as such until the collapse of the Soviet Union. During the Soviet period the Georgian economy was modernized and diversified. One of the most independence-minded republics, Georgia declared sovereignty on November 19, 1989, and independence on April 9, 1991. (Wikipedia)
Tsikhe
The Okros Tsikhe fortress was built in the late 13th or early 14th century and was one of the principal fortifications in possession of the Jaqeli dynasty of the Principality of Samtskhe. Owing to its dominant position in the Kvabliani valley, the fortress played a prominent role in the defense of Samtskhe against the invading Ottoman army during Lala Mustafa Pasha's Caucasian campaign in 1578. It was where the princess Dedisimedi had entrenched herself before negotiating a peace agreement with the Ottoman commander. After the final Ottoman conquest of the province, the fortress was known by its Turkish name, Altunkal'a, and served as the center of the homonymous district (liva). It served as a functional fortification till the end of the 18th century.

Medieval History
The Kingdom of Georgia reached its zenith in the 12th to early 13th centuries. This period during the reigns of David IV (r. 1089–1125) and his great-granddaughter Tamar (r. 1184–1213) has been widely termed as Georgia's Golden Age or the Georgian Renaissance. This early Georgian renaissance, which preceded its Western European analogue, was characterized by impressive military victories, territorial expansion, and a cultural renaissance in architecture, literature, philosophy and the sciences. The Golden age of Georgia left a legacy of great cathedrals, romantic poetry and literature, and the epic poem The Knight in the Panther's Skin, the latter which is considered a national epic. (Wikipedia)
Khevsur
Historically, Georgian highlander communities enjoyed a degree of autonomy. Khevsurs never accepted local lords; they elected their leaders or Khevisberi (ხევისბერი, elder) and council of elders and submitted themselves only to the monarch (see List of the Kings of Georgia). They were exceptional warriors with traditional Georgian qualities of courage, openness and honesty, fraternity, independence and love of freedom, who were often promoted as royal bodyguards. Kings regarded them as reliable guardians of the Caucasus Mountains and the northern border of the kingdom. In the battles Khevsurs wore flags adorned with crosses and considered themselves permanent members of the army of the sacred flags and guardians of Georgian Kings.

Cacicazgo
Cacicazgo is a phonetic Spanish transliteration (or a derivative) of the Taíno word for the lands ruled by a cacique. The Spanish colonial system recognized indigenous elites as nobles in Mexico and Peru, and other areas. Nobles could entail their estates, which were called cacicazgos on the model of Spanish entailed estates, or mayorazgos. This term is found in contexts such as "la princesa de Cofachiqui, señora de un cacigazgo indígena" or, for example: "In November of 1493, the island of Boriquén had approximately 20 cacigazgos." According to Spanish chronicles, the cacique was at the apex of the Taíno feudal structure. Bartolomé de las Casas refers to these cacigazgos as kingdoms. Many individual cacicazgos have been studied in colonial Mexico, showing that entailment was a successful means to preserve noble indigenous resources as the situation for commoners declined. There are cases where Spaniards married into cacique families, thereby giving them access to indigenous resources. In the Archivo General de la Nación, Mexico, a whole section of records, called Vínculos, is devoted to individual noble entailments. A collection of them was published in 1961. Cacicazgos survived into the nineteenth century. Conflicts over inheritance were common, and the litigants' arguments found in these cases form the basis for understanding some of the dynamics of the institution. Over time, the concept of cacique shifted, with some women attaining the title of cacica. Cacicazgo likewise underwent some transformation during the colonial era in Mexico. "By law, a cacique was a single heir and possessor of a cacicazgo estate, which always included land and often a subject labor force to work it. The Indians themselves, however, saw things differently, and by late colonial times it was not unusual for all the sons and daughters of a cacique (or cacica) to adopt the title. How and why this change took place, its chronology, and what it meant for local community organization remain imperfectly understood...The late colonial setting was vastly different, and indigenous noble claims of the period must be understood in the context in which they arose."[9]

History
Gran Colombia (Great Colombia) is a name used today for the state that encompassed much of northern South America and part of southern Central America from 1819 to 1831. This short-lived republic included the territories of present-day Colombia, Venezuela, Ecuador, Panama, northern Peru and northwest Brazil. The first three were the successor states to Gran Colombia at its dissolution. Panama was separated from Colombia in 1903. Since Gran Colombia's territory corresponded more or less to the original jurisdiction of the former Viceroyalty of New Granada, it also claimed the Caribbean coast of Costa Rica and Nicaragua, the Mosquito Coast, and Guayana Esequiba in Guyana. [NEWLINE][NEWLINE] Its existence was marked by a struggle between those who supported a centralized government with a strong presidency and those who supported a decentralized, federal form of government. At the same time, another political division emerged between those who supported the Constitution of Cucuta and two groups who sought to do away with the Constitution, either in favor of breaking up the nation into smaller republics or maintaining the union but creating an even stronger presidency. The faction that favored constitutional rule coalesced around Vice-President Francisco de Paula Santander, while those who supported the creation of a stronger presidency were led by President Simon Bolivar. The two men had been allies in the war against Spanish rule, but by 1825, their differences had become public and were an important part of the political instability from that year onward.

Simon Jose Antonio de la Santisima Trinidad Bolivar y Palacios Ponte y Blanco (24 July 1783 – 17 December 1830), commonly known as Simon Bolivar was a Venezuelan military and political leader. Bolivar played a key role in Latin America's successful struggle for independence from the Spanish Empire, and is today considered one of the most influential politicians in the history of the Americas. [NEWLINE][NEWLINE] Following the triumph over the Spanish monarchy, Bolivar participated in the foundation of the first union of independent nations in Hispanic-America, a republic, which was named Gran Colombia, of which he was president from 1819 to 1830. Bolivar remains regarded in Hispanic-America as a hero, visionary, revolutionary, and liberator. During his lifetime, he led Venezuela, Colombia (including Panama at the time), Ecuador, Peru (together with Don Jose de San Martin), and Bolivia to independence, and helped lay the foundations for democratic ideology in much of Latin America.

A llanero (Plainsman) is a Venezuelan or Colombian herder. The name is taken from the Llanos grasslands occupying western Venezuela and eastern Colombia. The Llanero were originally part Spanish and Indian and have a strong culture including a distinctive form of music. [NEWLINE][NEWLINE] During the wars of independence, Llaneros served in both armies and provided the bulk of the cavalry during the war. In 1819, an army of Llaneros, led by Simon Bolivar and Jose Antonio Paez, defeated the Spanish with a surprise attack when they crossed over the Orinoco plains and the Andes mountains.

Mysorean rockets were an Indian military weapon, the first iron-cased rockets successfully deployed for military use. The Mysorean army, under Hyder Ali and his son Tipu Sultan, used the rockets effectively against the British East India Company during the 1780s and 1790s. Their conflicts with the company exposed the British to this technology, which was then used to advance European rocketry with the development of the Congreve rocket in 1805.

During and after his many conquests, the Mauryan king Ashoka ordered the construction of numerous stone pillars across India. Those columns were between 12 to 15 metres high (40 to 50 feet) and were adorned with animal capitals, mostly with images of stylised lions. Also, the pillars were carved with inscriptions bearing the Edicts of Ashoka. The Edicts were the king's view of Dhamma, a set of social and religious rules, guidelines and policies. 3rd century BC brought the emergence of Buddhism, common use of iron and migration of rural populace into cities – those and more events thoroughly transformed Indian society. Ashoka's edicts, based on Buddhist thought, were aimed at providing solutions to growing internal problems, as well as at documenting the spread of Buddhism – both in India and beyond.

Kingdom of Mysore
History
The Kingdom of Mysore was a realm in southern India, traditionally believed to have been founded in 1399 in the vicinity of the modern city of Mysore. From 1799 until 1950, it was a princely state, until 1947 in a subsidiary alliance with British India. It then became Mysore State (later enlarged and renamed to Karnataka) with its ruler remaining as Rajapramukh until 1956, when he became the first Governor of the reformed state.
The kingdom, which was founded and ruled for most part by the Hindu Wodeyar family, initially served as a vassal state of the Vijayanagara Empire. The 17th century saw a steady expansion of its territory and during the rule of Narasaraja Wodeyar I and Chikka Devaraja Wodeyar, the kingdom annexed large expanses of what is now southern Karnataka and parts of Tamil Nadu to become a powerful state in the southern Deccan. During a brief Muslim rule, the kingdom shifted to a Sultanate style of administration.
During this time, it came into conflict with the Marathas, the Nizam of Hyderabad, the Kingdom of Travancore and the British, which culminated in the four Anglo-Mysore Wars. Success in the first Anglo-Mysore war and a stalemate in the second was followed by defeat in the third and the fourth. Following Tipu's death in the fourth war in the siege of Seringapatam (1799), large parts of his kingdom were annexed by the British, which signalled the end of a period of Mysorean hegemony over South India. The British restored the Wodeyars to their throne by way of a subsidiary alliance and the diminished Mysore was transformed into a princely state. The Wodeyars continued to rule the state until Indian independence in 1947, when Mysore acceded to the Union of India.
Even as a princely state, Mysore came to be counted among the more developed and urbanised regions of India. This period (1799–1947) also saw Mysore emerge as one of the important centres of art and culture in India. The Mysore kings were not only accomplished exponents of the fine arts and men of letters, they were enthusiastic patrons as well, and their legacies continue to influence rocket science, music, and art even today.

Sultan Hyder Ali
History
Hyder Ali, Haidarālī was the Sultan and de facto ruler of the Kingdom of Mysore in southern India. Born as Hyder Ali Khan, he distinguished himself militarily, eventually drawing the attention of Mysore's rulers. Rising to the post of Dalavayi (commander-in-chief) to Krishnaraja Wodeyar II, he came to dominate the titular monarch and the Mysore government. He became the de facto ruler of Mysore as Sarvadhikari (Chief Minister) by 1761. During intermittent conflicts against the East India Company during the First and Second Anglo–Mysore Wars, Hyder Ali distinguished himself in military tactics, being the innovator of military use of the iron-cased Mysorean rockets. He also significantly developed the Mysorean economy.
Though illiterate, Hyder Ali earned an important place in the history of southern India for his administrative acumen and military skills[citation needed]. He concluded an alliance with the French, and used the services of French workmen in raising his artillery and arsenal. His rule of Mysore was characterised by frequent warfare with his neighbours and rebellion within his territories. This was not unusual for the time as much of the Indian subcontinent was then in turmoil. He left his eldest son, Tipu Sultan, an extensive kingdom bordered by the Krishna River in the north, the Eastern Ghats in the east and the Arabian Sea in the west.
Maurya Empire
History
The Maurya Empire was an Iron Age power in ancient India. Established by Chandragupta Maurya in 322 BC, the Maurya Empire expanded westward, quickly claiming control of central and western India and exploiting the local disruptions due to Alexander the Great withdrawal. The Maurya Empire was the largest empire on the subcontinent and one of the largest in the world.
Terrain
Much of the Maurya Empire encompassed all of what is now India - the subcontinent is a large tropical plain bordered by the Himalaya Mountains, the Indian Ocean and the Arabian Sea. The peninsula itself is very flat and is littered with rivers cutting every which way across the plain, the largest of these being the Indus River.
Fallout from the Death of Alexander
The Maurya Empire was founded during what would turn out to be a tumultuous time; as Chandragupta Maurya and Chanakya, a Brahmin teacher from Takshashila traveled to Magadha - a large, powerful kingdom feared by its neighbors, the ever-growing power of Alexander the Great and his Macedonians refused to cross the River Beas to further push into India, deterred by the same fear of the Magadha. Alexander returned to Babylon and re-deployed the bulk of his forces west of the Indus river. When Alexander died in 323 BC his empire fractured, the local kings claimed independence and thus fought each other. This left several smaller satrapies in disunity, territories ripe for conquest.
Conquest of Magadha
Chanakya, made an advisor by Chandragupta, encouraged him and the army to claim the throne of Magadha. Chandragupta used his influence to discover many young men from the Magadha kingdom upset over the oppressive rule of the king Dhana and the resources for his long series of battles. In these ranks were the former general of Taxila, the representative of King Porus of Kakayee, and rulers of smaller states.[NEWLINE][NEWLINE]Preparing for the invasion of Pataliputra, Chandragupta developed a strategy. The Magadhan army drew out of the city to engage the Mauryan forces, meanwhile the Mauryan spies bribed the general of Nanda and caused civil unrest in the kingdom - the unrest led to the death of the heir to the throne. Chanakya was able to win popularity for Chandragupta. Nanda resigned, handing control of the city to the Mauryans. Chanakya then met with the prime minister of Magadha, Rakshasa and made him understand that his loyalty was not to the Nanda dynasty but Magadha, insisting he remain in office. Chanakya then threatened war that would cripple the kingdom. Rakshasa accepted and Chandragupta was made the King of Magadha, Rakshasa became his chief advisor and Chanakya an elder statesman.
Seleucid-Mauryan War
Chandragupta turned his attention to the Macedonians when Seleucus I Nicator, when trying to build the Seleucid Empire, tried to recapture the northwestern regions of India in 305 BC. Seleucus failed and the two rulers came to an agreement where the Greeks offered their princess and the satrapies of Paropamisade, Arachosia and Gedrosia, and the Mauryans offered 500 war elephants that ultimately played a role in Seleucus' victory in the Battle of Ipsus. Diplomacy was established with the Greeks and several Greeks such as Megasthenes, Deimakos and Dionysius lived at the Mauryan court. From this Chandragupta established a strong centralized state with a complex administration at Pataliputra. The historian Megasthenes described the city as being "surrounded by a wooden wall pierced by 64 gates and 570 towers - and rivaled the splendors of contemporaneous Persian sites such as Susa and Ecbatana."
Bindusara - the Blue Spot
Bindusara was the son of Chandragupta Maurya and his queen Durdhara; during his reign he would push the frontiers of the empire south. According to the Rajavalikatha - a Jain text - the original name of the emperor was Simhasena. The legend tells the tale of his birth; Chanakya used to feed Chandragupta small doses of poison in an effort to create an immunity against it should enemies attempt to poison him. One day, unaware of Chanakya's practices, Chandragupta shared his food with his pregnant wife who was a week away from delivery. Without this immunity the queen collapsed and died in just a few minutes. Chanakya entered just as she fell and, in order to save the unborn child, he immediately cut open her belly and took out the baby. A drop of poison already reached the baby and touched its head, discoloring his forehead with a permanent bluish spot - a "bindu". The young heir was thus named Bindusara.[NEWLINE][NEWLINE]At just 22 Bindusara inherited the Mauryan Empire - what is now regions of Northern, Central and Eastern India and parts of Afghanistan and Baluchistan. Bindusara expanded to the southern regions of India, as far as what is now Karnataka. He brought sixteen states under Mauryan control and conquered almost the entire Indian peninsula, he is said to have claimed the 'land between the two seas' - this is the peninsula area between the Bay of Bengal and the Arabian Sea. Apart from the friendly Dravidian kingdoms of the Cholas, the Pandyas and Cheras, the only southern kingdom that did not fall to Bindusara was Kalinga in modern Odisha.[NEWLINE][NEWLINE]Bindusara's life is not well documented; Chanaka continued to serve as prime minister during his reign. According to the Tibetan scholar Taranatha when he visited India, Chanakya helped Bindusara "to destroy the noble kings of the sixteen kingdoms and thus become absolute master of the territory between the eastern and western oceans." The citizens of Taxila revolted twice during his rule; first was the maladministration of Suseema, Bindusara's eldest son. The reason for the second revolt is not known, but Bindusara could not suppress it in his lifetime. He died in 272 BC and was succeeded by his son Ashokavardhan Maurya, more commonly known as Ashoka the Great.
Ashokavardhan the Great
As a young prince Ashoka was an impressive commander, crushing the revolts in Ujjain and Taxila. As a monarch he was bold and aggressive, re-asserting the empire's superiority in the south and west; for more on his conquests and his life in general see his Civilopedia entry. However it was between 262 and 261 BC where a pivotal event changed Ashoka's life - the conquest of Kalinga. Ashoka's forces won overwhelmingly, yet the fact that approximately 100,000 soldiers and citizens were killed in the battle, including 10,000 of Ashoka's men, wrangled Ashoka. Hundreds of thousands of people had become affected by the fallout of the battle, witnessing this himself Ashoka felt remorseful - so much so that even with the annexation of Kalinga Ashoka accepted and embraced Buddhism, renouncing violence and war. He sent out missionaries to travel all over Asia to spread Buddhism to other civilizations.[NEWLINE][NEWLINE]Ashoka established principles of 'ahimsa' - meaning 'to do no harm' - by banning hunting and violent sport, and ending indentured and forced labor - thousands of people in Kalinga had been forced into hard labor and servitude. Even though he did maintain an army, mainly to keep the peace and authority, Ashoka extended friendly relations with countries across Europe and Asia, sponsoring Buddhist missions. Ashoka undertook a large public works campaign across the empire. With over four decades of peace, harmony and prosperity during his reign Ashoka is one of the most successful and famous kings in Indian history and remains an idealized figure of inspiration in the country today.[NEWLINE][NEWLINE]The Edicts of Ashoka are set in stones throughout the Subcontinent; as far west as Afghanistan and as far south as Andhra. The edicts state his laws and accomplishments during his reign. The edicts also attest to Ashoka having sent envoys to the Greek rulers in the West as far as the Mediterranean, going so far as to name each of the rulers of the Hellenic world at the time such as 'Amtiyoko', 'Tulamaya' and 'Alikasudaro' - Antiochus, Ptolemy and Alexander respectively.
Decline and the Indo-Greek Kingdom
After Ashoka's death in 232 BC followed 50 years of weaker kings. Brihadratha was the last Mauryan ruler of the dynasty and held a nation much smaller from Ashoka's reign, though he still upheld the Buddhist faith. Brihadratha was assassinated in 185 BC during a military parade by the Brahmin general Pusyamitra Sunga, the commander of his guard, who then took the throne and established the Sunga dynasty. Buddhist records write that the assassination and the rise of the Sunga empire led to a wave of persecution against Buddhists and a resurgence of Hinduism. Scholars tend to differ as to the legitimacy of these records.[NEWLINE][NEWLINE]The fall of the Mauryans left the Khyber Pass unguarded and a wave of foreign invasion followed soon after. The Greco-Bactrian king Demetrius capitalized on the break up and took southern Afghanistan and parts of northern India by about c. 180 BC, creating the Indo-Greek Kingdom. The Indo-Greeks maintained the land in the trans-Indus region and raided parts of central India for about a century until roughly c. 70 BC when the Indo-Scythians invaded and succeeded.

Samraat Chakravartin
History
Ashoka Maurya was an emperor of the Maurya dynasty and one of the greatest leaders in Indian history. He originally stretched the empire to cover nearly the entire subcontinent; from Khorasan and parts of ancient Afghanistan, through the Hindu Kush mountains to Bangladesh and Assam and as far south as Kerala and Andhra Pradesh. However Ashoka is mostly remembered for the battle against Kalinga where he ultimately adopted Buddhism and renounced violence. In his edicts Ashoka is referred to as Devanampriya - "the Beloved of the Gods" - and Priyadarsin - "He who regards everyone with affection".
Early Life and Reign
Born in the capital of Pataliputra, Ashoka was the son of emperor Bindusara and Dharma, a lower ranked wife of his, although texts tend to differ over his mother; the Avadana suggest his mother to be Queen Subhadrang. It is from her exclamation "I am now without sorrow," where Ashoka got his name. The Divyavadana tells a similar story, the queen is named Janapadakalyani. Ashoka had several older siblings; all of them were half-brothers from Bindusara's other wives. As a child his fighting abilities were apparent, where he received royal military training. Ashoka was known as a fearsome hunter; legend suggests that he killed a lion with just a wooden stick. Due to this reputation of a fierce warrior and a heartless general Ashoka was sent to quash the riots in the Avanti province of the empire.[NEWLINE][NEWLINE]The Divyavadana continues to tell Ashoka's story, the text describes Ashoka putting down a revolt caused by the activities of corrupt ministers. Chanakya, one of Bindusara's great lords - and the same lord who advised Chandragupta Maurya - destroyed the nobles and kings of 16 towns and laid claim to all the land between the eastern and western seas. Historians differ as to the proceeding events that ensued as a result; most understand this as an indication of Bindusara's conquest of the Deccan. Nonetheless following the suppression of the revolt Ashoka was stationed at Ujjayini as governor. Bindusara's death by 273 BC led to a war over succession. The Divyavadana tells that Bindusara wanted his son Sushim to succeed, but Ashoka was supported by the late emperor's ministers, suggesting Sushim as arrogant and disrespectful. One of the ministers, Radhagupta played a very important role in Ashoka's rise. The Ashokavadana recounts Radhagupta offering Ashoka an old royal elephant for him to ride to the Garden of the Gold Pavilion where King Bindusara would determine his successor. Afterwards Ashoka got rid of the legitimate heir to the throne by tricking him into entering a pit full of live coals. According to the Ashokavadana Radhagupta would be appointed prime minister by Ashoka once he secured the throne - four years after his succession Ashoka was coronated in 269 BC.[NEWLINE][NEWLINE]Buddhist texts suggest that Ashoka was of a terrible nature and a bad temper - however Professor Charles Derekmeier cautions that these texts intend to dramatize the change that the religion brought to him, and thus exaggerate Ashoka's past after his conversion. What is known is that as Ashoka ascended the throne he expanded the empire over the next eight years - up to the present-day borders of Burma and Bangladesh, and the state of Assam in India in the east to present-day Iran, Persia and Afghanistan in the west. From the Pamir Knots in the north to very nearly the tip of the peninsula at southern India.
Kalinga - the Battle that Changed Everything
Of Ashoka's conquests as emperor of the Mauryan empire the Kalinga War is his most famous victory, but not from the tactics of the battle nor the valor of the men. During his reign Kalinga was a state that prided its sovereignty and democracy. As a monarchical parliamentary democracy the state was unique in ancient Bharata - the state adopted 'Rajdharma', meaning 'the duty of the rulers', which was entwined with bravery and dharma. Ashoka invaded the state and annexed it with relative ease, but as he cavorted the streets, basking in his victory, he was moved by the sheer number of bodies littering the ground - over 100,000 men fell in battle; 10,000 of which were Ashoka's own men, as well as a number of civilians rallying to defend Kalinga - and the wails of the kith and kin of the dead - the battle displaced more than 150,000 citizens.[NEWLINE][NEWLINE]So touched and remorseful was Ashoka that he converted to Buddhism, rejecting violence and conquest and replacing it with peace and harmony. This ultimately led to massive expansion of the religion by Ashoka in the Mauryan empire and beyond at about c. 250 BC. His son and daughter - Mahinda and Sanghamitra respectively - later continued his expansion of Buddhism by establishing it in Ceylon, what is now Sri Lanka.
Forty Peaceful Years
After the annexation of Kalinga and his conversation to Buddhism, Ashoka returned to his throne and ensured peace and friendly relations through the rest of his rule. Forty years past, and in that time Ashoka established a golden age in the empire.[NEWLINE][NEWLINE]Ashoka believed that Buddhism is beneficial for all man and animal-kind as well as the plant life, this belief encouraged the construction of many stupas, viharas, chaitya and other residences for Buddhist monks across the empire - according to the Ashokavadana he ordered the creation of 84,000 stupas to hold the Buddha's relics. He gave donations to viharas and mathas, sent his son and daughter to Sri Lanka to spread the religion, and also sent prominent Buddhist monks to present-day Kashmir, Afghanistan, Syria, Persia, Egypt, Greece, Italy, Turkey, Nepal, Bhutan, China, Mongolia, Cambodia, Laos, Burma, Thailand and Vietnam - Ashoka single-handedly spread Buddhism to all of the known world. Ashoka is also well known to have sent emissaries to transmit messages or letters to various people in the wider world. It was not unusual to add oral messages to the letters and these were used to spread his dhammavijaya - his victory through dhrama, which he saw as his greatest victory. Greeks living in the empire were also active in spreading Buddhism - some of Ashoka's emissaries are described in Pali sources as leading Greek Buddhist monks.[NEWLINE][NEWLINE]Domestically Ashoka held strong might until his conversion where he maintained friendlier ties with the frontier kingdoms. His edicts tell us that he provided medical treatment for humans and animals in and out of the empire, and built wells and planted trees along the roads to benefit his people. Ashoka banned the slaughter and consumption of cattle and imposed restriction on fishing and eating fish. By banning hunting, creative veterinary clinics and removed eating meat on many holidays the Mauryan Empire under Ashoka is described as "one of the few instances in world history of a government treating its animals as citizens who are as deserving of its protection as the human residents."[NEWLINE][NEWLINE]Ashokmudra, the Lion Capital of Ashoka is a sculpture of four Indian lions standing back to back. Originally it rested atop the Aśoka pillar in Sarnath, while the pillar still stands in its original location the Lion Capital is now in the Sarnath Museum. The Lion Capital has been adopted as the Indian national emblem and the "Ashoka Chakra", a Buddhist motif found at the Lion Capital's base, was adopted into the Indian flag in its center. Carved from a single block of polished sandstone, the capital contains the four lions mounted on an abacus, with a frieze carrying sculptures of an elephant, a horse, a bull and a lion by istelf, all separated by spoked chariot wheels over a bell-shaped lotus. The animals represent the different steps of Buddha's life; the elephant symbolizes Buddha's idea, referring to the dream of Queen Maya of a white elephant entering her womb. The bull represents desire during his life as a prince. The horse displays Buddha's departure from life in the palace. The lion represents his accomplishments. Other construction efforts from Ashoka include the Mahabodhi Temple in Bihar, Bhir Mound in Taxila and Butkara Stupa in Swat.
Death and Rediscovery
At the age of 72 Ashoka died in 232 BC. Legend says his body burned for seven days and nights during his cremation, however we know that his ashes were spread across the Ganges River possibly as Varanasi less than a day after his death. The reign of Ashoka was very nearly lost to the world, he left no record of his reign apart from the sculpted pillars found all around what was the empire. The pillars inscribed his actions and teachings he wanted to publish under his name, as a result of this Ashoka left behind the Prakrit language, the first written language in the subcontinent since the ancient Harappa. Just ten of the Ashokstambha - Pillars of Ashoka - survive with inscriptions. The first Ashokstambha was found in the 16th century by English traveler Thomas Coryat in the ruins of ancient Delhi.
Judgement of History
Ashoka was without doubt one of the greatest leaders in Indian history, originally a mighty warrior and tactician Ashoka is more well known for his dramatic and iconic turnaround from an aggressor to a pacifist. His far-reaching spread of Buddhism and friendly banter to other kingdoms held the happiness of the people and kept the peace of the empire. One of Ashoka's most endearing legacies, Buddhist kingship is still present today in Thailand through the traditional role of the Thai king as a religious and secular leader.

Philippine Empire
History
The Philippine Republic, more commonly known as the First Philippine Republic or the Malolos Republic, was a nascent revolutionary government in the Philippines. It was formally established with the proclamation of the Malolos Constitution on January 23, 1899, in Malolos, Bulacan,[Note 1] and endured until the capture of President Emilio Aguinaldo by the American forces on March 23, 1901, in Palanan, Isabela, which effectively dissolved the First Republic. The First Philippine Republic was established after the Philippine Revolution against Spanish Empire (1896-1897) and the Spanish–American War between Spain and the United States (1898). Following the American victory at the Battle of Manila Bay, Aguinaldo returned to the Philippines, issued the Philippine Declaration of Independence on June 12, 1898, and established a revolutionary Philippine government. In December 1898, Spain sold the Philippines to the United States in the 1898 Treaty of Paris, making the United States formally the Philippines colonial power. The Malolos Constitution establishing the First Philippine Republic was proclaimed the following month. The Philippine–American War began in February 1899, which the Philippine Republic lost. The Philippine Republic was the first constitutional republic in Asia. Although there were several Asian republics predating the First Philippine Republic for example, the Republic of Formosa or the Republic of Ezo, the Republic at Malolos was the first to frame a comprehensive constitution duly approved by a partially elected congress.

Emilio Aguinaldo
History
Emilio Aguinaldo y Famy was a Filipino revolutionary, politician, and a military leader who is officially recognized as the first and the youngest President of the Philippines (1899–1901) and first president of a constitutional republic in Asia. He led Philippine forces first against Spain in the latter part of the Philippine Revolution (1896–1898), and then in the Spanish–American War (1898), and finally against the United States during the Philippine–American War (1899–1901). He was captured in Palanan, Isabela by American forces on March 23, 1901, which brought an end to his presidency.[NEWLINE][NEWLINE] In 1935, Aguinaldo ran unsuccessfully for president of the Philippine Commonwealth against Manuel Quezon. After the Japanese invasion of the Philippines in 1941, he cooperated with the new rulers, even making a radio appeal for the surrender of the American and Filipino forces on Bataan. He was arrested as a collaborator after the Americans returned but was later freed in a general amnesty and was subsequently exonerated.

Rock-Cut Tomb
Perhaps the best known feature of Nabataean culture were the intricate rock-cut façades of their tombs. The tomb façades draw upon a rich array of Hellenistic and Near Eastern architecture and, in this sense, their architecture reflects the diverse and different cultures with which the Nabateans traded, interacted, and even intermarried (King Aretas IV''s daughter was married to Herod Antipas, the son of Herod the Great, whose mother was also Nabataean). Many of the tombs contain niches or small chambers for burials, cut into the stone walls. No human remains have ever been found in any of the tombs, and the exact funerary practices of the Nabataeans remain unknown.

History
The Nabataeans, also Nabateans were an Arab people who inhabited northern Arabia and the Southern Levant, and whose settlements, most prominently the assumed capital city of Raqmu, now called Petra, in AD 37 – c. 100, gave the name of Nabatene to the borderland between Arabia and Syria, from the Euphrates to the Red Sea. Their loosely controlled trading network, which centered on strings of oases that they controlled, where agriculture was intensively practiced in limited areas, and on the routes that linked them, had no securely defined boundaries in the surrounding desert. Trajan conquered the Nabataean kingdom, annexing it to the Roman Empire, where their individual culture, easily identified by their characteristic finely potted painted ceramics, became dispersed in the general Greco-Roman culture and was eventually lost. They were later converted to Christianity. Jane Taylor, a writer, describes them as "one of the most gifted peoples of the ancient world"

Moorish Empire
Moors
History
The Iberian Peninsula today is owned completely by Spain and Portugal, with the exception of the British rule in Gibraltar, but for years they had been dominated my an outside power. These people were known as the Moors; Arabs, though mainly hailing from Morocco. For years, they waged war against the crumbling Christian kingdoms in the region, overcoming them quickly, and soon establishing a centre of power in the city of Cordoba. This city became one of the most well-known settlements in the region the Arabs called Al-Andalus, and was famed for its wealth, arts and even religious tolerance. However, Christian piety took off in the remnants of Christian Spain, and they vengefully attacked the Moorish cities as part of the Reconquista, overcoming the last settlement in 1492. This ended 500 years of Moorish rule, and put an end to the tolerance that was once valued within Cordoba for hundreds of years.
Geography
The Cordoban and Moorish settlement was very diverse, in the sense that it spanned multiple continents. In North Africa, the origin of the Moorish people, the land was dominated by desert sands. This means that the Moors were very used to hot temperatures, which certainly paid off in Andalusia; the region that the Moors conquered here was very warm, and the central belt of the peninsula was almost a barren wasteland, yet the Moors still managed to settle the land effectively. Even the city of Cordoba was built on these plains; and as you will soon see, the city managed to prosper even within difficult terrain, which should be attributed to the Moorish background. Overall, Al-Andalus was the perfect second home for these new settlers from North Africa.
Before Iberia
For years, the Moors had been pounding at the gates of Iberia. Beginning in 711, the Moors, mainly from Morocco, decided to invade the entire peninsula, their presence growing ever stronger in the world. Winning battle after battle against the fragmented Christian kingdoms, the Moors were eventually able to advance to the point where they had majority control of Iberia. They probably would have taken the entire region, had it not been for the decisive Battle of Poitiers, where the Moors suffered their first major defeat at the hands of the Frankish general Charles Martel, effectively saving Christendom from Islamic domination. During this time it is important to note that much of modern-day Spain and Portugal was controlled not from the region itself, but from the Umayyad capital of Damascus; however, this was soon to change.
Establishment of Cordoba
In 750, the Moorish presence in Iberia was at its greatest extent. However, they were still controlled from Damascus – albeit not for long. The title of Caliph was removed from the Umayyads in Damascus, thus leading to no external control over the Moorish settlement; in 756, Abd-ar-Rahman I proclaimed himself Emir of Cordoba, and in that action, creating the predecessor to the Caliphate. Soon afterwards, he had to deal with several threats to his reign, seeing off each one, and soon after, he managed to get control of most of the Moors, not just in Iberia, but in North Africa as well. Though he was not highly favoured in the Umayyad court, he managed to get enough approval from his people for him to stay in his post. During his reign, the now-independent Cordoba began to thrive.

The Qasimi claim descent from the Prophet Muhammad but only became active in the 18th century when the Yaruba dynasty was dissolved. [NEWLINE] [NEWLINE] The Persian gulf was, as now, an important shipping lane for goods from the far East, most importantly the British Raj. The Qasimi pirates quickly became enemies of the British Empire as they grew into a force able to assert control over this lane. Keen to secure the route for goods to flow from India to Europe, the British began a campaign in the 19th century to Eradicate the Qasimi pirates. In 1808 the British deployed 3 warships to the region as a show of force, but that same year an enormous fleet of Qasimi raiders began attacking ships off the Indian coast, seizing a large British ship, the HMS Minerva, and conerting it to the flagship of the Al Qawaseem. At that time it was estimated that the Qasimi had a fleet of 60 large oceangoing warships, 800 smaller armed Dhows and nearly 20,000 men - all this against 2 British warships. [NEWLINE] [NEWLINE] Following the disaster, and amid the news that a further 20,000 bedouin warriors had unfurled their banners and marched to join the Qawasim in the event of a land war, the British assembled a force with the aim of raiding several pirate bases from the sea. In November, the flotilla shelled several key positions and sank many Arab ships before landing a raiding party in Ras-Al-Khaimah, sacking the town and burning 30 large warships in the harbour alongside 20 smaller dhows. The raid severely weakened the Qawaseem and their piracy greatly decreased in later years.
