The United Arab Emirates
History
The UAE rose from humble origins as an undeveloped backwater on the edge of an inhospitable desert, to a regional power and one of the richest nations on earth. Perhaps most famously, the UAE has pumped their millions into some of the most awe-inspiring constructions of the modern world and Dubai itself, the nations largest city, has become a byword for ridiculous wealth, beauty and culture - truly the pearl of the Arab gulf.
Geography and Climate
The United Arab Emirates is nestled in the eastern half of the Persian gulf, on the edge of the Arabian Desert. Specifically, the UAE teeters on the edge of a particulously barren section of the desert known somewhat forebodingly as the Rub Al-Khali, or, in English - 'The Empty Quarter'. As such, the UAE is swelteringly hot, particularly in the long summer months. Frequently the temperature rolls into the 50's (120+ Farenheit) during the summer, and tends towards the low 30's or 20's during the cooler months. Nourishing currents from the Persian gulf ensure that the area remains fit for habitation however, and today much of the UAE is fairly green (albeit with the assistance of considerable manmade irrigation devices) and is certainly more populated than the inland regions bordering the nation in Saudi Arabia. The UAE also features several important Oases - Liwa Oasis is one of the largest and most important in the Arabian peninsula and has sustained life for thousands of years. There is not a single river in the UAE.
Origins
Despite its inhospitable climate, the UAE has been inhabited for tens of thousands of years. Southern Arabia is often posited as the location where humans first left Africa, roving along the coastlines in small bands. Indeed, stone tools from the UAE have been dated as far back as 125,000 BC and there is evidence to support an even earlier habitation. Some of the earliest accounts of the region come from Mesopatamia, which was a prominent trading partner of the tribes and city-states that dotted the Persian gulf, possibly trading the extensive copper reserves of the Hajjar mountains. Julfar, one of the few named towns from this period in the UAE, grew into an important trading city and was used as a vital base for the Arab invasion of Persia in the 7th century AD. [NEWLINE] [NEWLINE] Islamic historiography contends that the UAE, along with the rest of the Bahrain region, adopted Islam in 628 upon receiving a letter from the Prophet Muhammad. The Prophet sent various letters to monarchs around the world inviting them to join Islam and it seems that his letter to the people of Bahrain and Oman is the only one to have had serious consequences - the Caesar of Byzantium, the Shah of Persia, the Negus of Ethiopia and various provincial governors of the Roman Empire all turned him down. The letter read as follows, [NEWLINE] [NEWLINE] In the name of God the Beneficent, the Merciful: From Muhammad the Prophet of God to Munzir bin Sawa, may peace be on you! I praise God, who is one and there none to be worshiped but except him. I bear evidence that there is no God but God and that Muhammad is a servant of God and His Prophet. Thereafter I remind you of God. Whoever accepts admonition does it for his own good. Whoever followed my messengers and acted in accordance their guidance; he, in fact,followed me and accepted my advice. My messengers have highly praised your behavior. You shall continue in your present office. You should remain faithful to Allah and his Prophet. I accept your recommendation regarding the people of Bahrain. I forgive the offenses of the offenders. Therefore, you may also forgive them of the people of Bahrain whoever want to continue in their Jewish or Majusi faith, should be made to pay Jizia. Seal: God’s Prophet Muhammad. [NEWLINE] [NEWLINE] Upon adopting Islam, the people of the UAE rose up against the Persians who dominated the region and joined themselves to Muhammad's new caliphate. Despite this, many tribes and clans declared their independence in the brutal Ridda Wars after Muhammads death. Claiming that they had pledged allegience to Muhammad, not to his successors, many refused to recognise the authority of a post-Muhammad caliphate, leading Abu Bakr to dispatch a large army to the region in November of 632. The ensuing battle cost, allegedly, 10,00 lives - a large graveyard in Dibba, the UAE, still stands to this day to commemorate the slaughter. After this, the region was integrated into the new caliphate.
The Era of Piracy
Following the gradual disintegration of central control in the late 9th and 10th century, the gulf region fell under the sway of various local and external factions. In 899 the Qamratians, a violent and bizarre sect of Islam, seized the gulf coast and declared an independent republic. The Qamratians went on to forcibly extract tribute from the caliphate, pillage most of Iraq and most daringly, sack Mecca! The sect stole the Qaaba, ransoming it back to the caliphate in 952. After the collapse of the Qarmatians, the UAE fell back into relative obscurity much like the rest of the Arabian peninsula, until the Europeans arrived sometime in the 16th century. [NEWLINE] [NEWLINE] The Portugeuse briefly laid claim to the region, constructing a fort in Dibba, (Debe) but real control remained in the hands of local tribes. Sometime in the 18th century, foreign control of the region waned to the point where a new tribe - the Qawaseem - declared a free kingdom of Sharjah, Ras-Al-Khaimah and Lengeh (in modern Persia) and began an era of unrestricted piracy in the gulf. Quickly the region became known as the infamous 'Pirate Coast' as Qasimi ships plundered their way to riches unimaginable. Vital British shipping from India and the far east flowed through the gulf and the Qawaseem grew fat off of its booty - by 1809 the Qawaseem warfleet numbered at almost 100 large warships (Baghlah) and around 800 smaller gunboats (Dhows). For comparison, the British navy at the time had 3 warships (A Ship of the line and 2 frigates) in the region. Despite this size disparity, the British soon tired of the Qasimi raiding and sent a much larger force to Ras-Al-Khaimah in November of 1809. The fleet sacked the town and burned most of the ships in the harbour, before sailing down the coast and bombarding multiple known pirate hideouts. After a similar operation in 1819, this time armed with updated maps of the region, the local sheikhs were forced to concede to the superior British navy.
British Era
Following their utter humiliation at the hands of the British fleet, the various sheikhs of the region began to sign treaties with the British comitting themselves to combatting illegal piracy and slave-trading. The readiness of these sheikhs to align themselves with the European powers gave rise to the term 'Trucial Oman' or 'Trucial States' to describe the region, especially after 2 further treaties in 1843 and 1853. Closer integration with Britain followed an 1892 'Exclusivity Agreement', in which the Emirs and Sheikhs of the UAE agreed not to enter relationships with other foreign powers and in return gained protection from the British warfleet. The relative stability this brought to the gulf allowed an explosion in trade and, above all, the pearl industry. With the waves now largely calm and piracy-free, thousands of emiratis took to the waters to fish for pearls, which were in high demand among the upper classes in Europe. [NEWLINE] [NEWLINE] The Pearl trade allowed the region to grow, particularly towns such as Sharjah and Abu Dhabi. At the time, pearl-diving was a dangerous activity; the only way to collect pearls was to manually swim to the ocean floor (often 100 feet deep or more on a single breath) to collect oysters. They would then be brought to the surface and searched, though it would often require up to a tonne of oysters to find 3 or 4 pearls. All this made pearls incredibly expensive, so although the work was dangerous and rarely bore fruit, it brought considerable wealth to the region. Until, in the 1920's, the Great depression and the invention of the cultured pearl in Japan wiped out the industry. [NEWLINE] [NEWLINE] Despite the setback, and a few decades of sever economic depression in the region, the UAE was about to stumble upon a treasure trove of something far more valuable than pearls - oil. Starting in 1935, local Sheikhs began to consent to grant rights for oil companies to survey the area for reserves. Despite the first drill turning up dry at a staggering cost of £1M, an offshore drilling in 1958 finally yielded results. Money began to flow into the states coffers and Sheikh Zayed began a massive campaign of modernisation and diversification. In 1969, Dubai too yeilded oil and the sheikh, Rashid bin Saeed Al Maktoum, began a series of projects aiming to turn Dubai into a truly global city.
Independence and Federation
Despite the tremendous wealth now flowing out of the region, the United Kingdom began to dismantle its overseas empire. In 1968, prime minister Harold Wilson announced that the UK would seek to end its relationship with the Trucial States, not least because of the extraordinary cost of keeping a fleet deployed in the Persian gulf, and the rise of Iran. Wary of the isolated position of the UAE, Sheikh Zayed, ruler of Abu Dhabi, offered to pay for the entire cost of keeping the British navy in the region, but was turned down. In March of 1971, Edward Heath warned the states to begin preparations for independence. Reluctantly, the nine emirates of the Trucial states (the seven emirates of the modern UAE plus Bahrain and Qatar) began negotiations for a federation, but could not agree on terms. They were spurred into action when, just a day before they were due to become officially independent, an Iranian destroyer seized the Tunb islands. Fearing their exposed vulnerability, Dubai and Abu Dhabi agreed to enter a federation together and on the 2nd of December 1971, the other Emirates were invited to join. Though Bahrain and Qatar declined this invitation, the remaining emirates formed the United Arab Emirates and began preparations for their new union.
Modern Times
Following this, the new nation began heavily investing its immense oil revenues. Particularly Dubai, which attempted to diversify its economy to avoid overdependence on oil revenue. By the dawn of the 21st century, the UAE had begun to attract businesses from all over the world and its two main cities - Dubai and Abu Dhabi, had grown into major global destinations. Most notably, the UAE has poured millions into the construction of immense wonders such as the Burj Dubai, the Burj Khalifa and the Palm Jumeirah. Though badly hit by the 2008 financial crash, the UAE weathered the Arab spring with little to no incedent and continued to grow at record speeds. The UAE has participated in combat operations against Afghanistan in 2001, Iraq in 2003 and Libya in 2011 and contiues to debate participation in the Syrian civil war. Though still a monarchy, the first ever elections in the UAE were held in 2006 and the movement for increased political representation is growing among middle-class Emiratis. Despite all this, the nation has faced allegations of migrant worker mistreatment, gender inequality and is largely criticised for the role of Shariah law in its legal system.
UAE Factoids
Not all Emirates are created equal - Abu Dhabi, the UAE's largest emirate, encompasses 87% of the nations land area, whereas the smallest, Ajman, is a mere 100 square miles, 0.3% of the land area. [NEWLINE][NEWLINE] Only about 9% of the UAE's population is native to the country, the other 91% is comprised of immigrants from dozens of countries, with India providing the most. [NEWLINE][NEWLINE] The Dubai Police owns several lambourghinis, ferrarris and bentleys for high speed chases. [NEWLINE][NEWLINE] ALL of the worlds top 5 highest skyscrapers are in Dubai, and 7 out of the top 10 highest. [NEWLINE][NEWLINE] There are no personal taxes in the UAE. [NEWLINE][NEWLINE]

History
Sheikh Zayed's remarkable life saw him rise from the fourth son of a lowly sheikh in Al Ain who couldn't even afford to go to school, to one of the richest and most powerful men in the middle east. Rather than merely accept the gifts thrust upon him in his life, he actively campaigned to raise the station of his countrymen and remains known as a true 'man of the people' in modern middle-eastern political discourse. In an era of corrupt, cruel and innefectual leaders throughout the Islamic world, Sheikh Zayed was able to remain fair and tolerant, while growing his country to quickly surpass almost all of his contemporaries. An archetypal benign monarch, Zayed truly shaped the modern world to his image.
Early Life
Sheikh Zayed was born in Abu Dhabi on March 6th 1918 as the fourth, and youngest, son of the Emir of Abu Dhabi - Sheikh Sultan bin Zayed bin Khalifah Al Nahyan. Despite their royal status, the Al-Nahyans were desperately poor and, as the fourth son, Sheikh Zayed was not sent to school and instructed in the basics of Islam. In 1927 Zayed was sent to Al Ain, further inland, to learn the ways of the Bedouin. Al Ain was situated on the crucial Al Buraimi Oasis and was an important station for the nomadic Bedouin tribes of the Emirati desert. Under their tutelage, Zayed was schooled in the ways of the desert and how to survive in such a harsh environment. Zayed was later appointed as the governor of eastern Abu Dhabi, continuing to operate out of Al Ain. Mostly desert, the position was extremely difficult. He ruled the poorest part of the nation, prone to serious disease outbreaks and wracked by starvation and poverty.
The Oil Years
Sheikh Zayed quickly noticed the serious problems with the region and assisted oil companies with surveys in the hope of finding deposits of the valuable resource. Quickly however, the emirate's neighbours began to realise the value of the trucial coast and attempted to make various land claims. In 1952 a group of Saudi scouts seized the oasis and declared the village of Hamasa to be a part of Saudi territory. (and with it, the vast oil reserves beneath the territory.) Many attempts were made to force Zayed to back down but he refused to compromise the territorial integrity of his state and rejected a £30M bribe from parties interested in claiming the land (For reference, 30 million pounds in 1952 was equal to about one billion dollars today.) Zayed and his brother traveled to Geneva to attempt to settle the dispute but allegations of Saudi bribery among judges quickly soured the conference and the two pulled out and returned to Arabia. Instead, Zayed appealed to his British suzerains and the oasis was occupied in a tense operation by the trucial Oman levies. Bloodshed was avoided and Zayed took personal control of the area, developing the irrigation systems and working on establishing his own contacts in the oil industry. [NEWLINE] [NEWLINE] In 1958, oil was finally discovered in the emirate. Despite this however, the innefectual sheikh Shakhbut bin Sultan Al Nahyan, Zayeds brother, refused to properly use the royalties from oil exports to benefit the area effectively and in 1966 Zayed deposed him in a bloodless coup, vowing to use the money to improve Abu Dhabis standing. Shakhbut was flown to London and was allowed to return to the UAE in the 1970s. Immedeately, Zayed began making plans to elevate the nation and hired a Japanese architect to design a capital city worthy of a major power yet trouble beset Zayeds rule almost instantly. In January 1968, the British foreign minister announced to a room of shocked Emirati sheikhs that the United Kingdom would begin preparations to sever all ties with the Trucial gulf and end its protection of the region. Fearing for the gulfs independence, Zayed offered to pay for the entire cost of the British navy in the Persian Gulf personally, but was turned down. Instead, Zayed drove to the border of Abu Dhabi and Dubai, where he met Sheikh Rashid bin Saeed Al Maktoum of Dubai. The two agreed that they would begin preparing to unite their two nations in an effort to preserve the independence of the trucial coast after the British exodus.
The Federation
Tense negotiations soon followed this agreement. Zayed was a firm believer in the principle of honest, open negotiations but the talks soon stalemated as the various states of the Persian gulf disagreed over the terms of a hypothetical union. The bickering was ended however when, on December 1st 1971, an iranian destroyer broke formation and seized the disputed Tunb islands from the emirate of Sharjah. The islands themselves were largely unimportant but it was a clear display of arrogance from Tehran, the message was clear: an independent tiny emirate was no match for her neighbours, and were vulnerable to open bullying. Shocked, Dubai and Abu Dhabi confirmed that, nomatter what happened upon independence, they would unite. The next day, the two extended their invitations to the other emirates, forming the UAE. (Bahrain and Qatr declined to join however, and remain independent.) [NEWLINE] [NEWLINE] Upon the formation of this new union, Zayed set out his vision for the future. The vast oil revenues of the Persian gulf were set to constructing schools, hospitals and roads, while Zayed made overtures to various international businesses, offering 0% tax tates and prime real estate to any businesses thinking of doing business in the new nation. Throughout the 70s and 80s, Zayed affirmed his conviction to (relative) liberalism despite the corruption and cruelty spreading throughout the Arab world. Zayed allowed free worship and permitted free media, though expected most media organisations within the UAE to self-censor and not insult the country or its rulers. Allowances were made to allow expat cultures to flower within the country, and Zayed drew scorn and criticism from many Arab government figures both inside and outside the UAE for his permissive stances on foreign cultures and religions and his liberal attitudes towards the rights of women. He considered himslef a 'Man of the People' and despite his vocal displeasure for Saddams regime in Iraq, denounced the sanctions for causing unfair suffering and starvation despite the lack of pressure on the Iraqi government, causing a storm of controversy with the UAE's close ally, Kuwait. [NEWLINE] [NEWLINE] Zayed directed considerable amounts of wealth towards aiding the less fortunate and made all hospitals, schools and universities free for UAE ciztizens, despite the 0% personal tax rate. He is also locally known as the 'Man who turned the desert green' for his extensive work in irrigating the harsh emirati desert - he is the reason that Dubai and Abu Dhabi today are lined with thousands of trees and flowers growing freely from across the world. He even set up a fund which gave money to the poorest arab nations which continues today. Despite all this genoristy, Zayed remained one of the worlds most wealthy men until is death in 2004 - at one point, the UAE sat on a tenth of the worlds proven oil reserves.
Verdict of History
There are few 'Rags to Riches' stories as captivating and incredible as Sheikh Zayeds. From the fourth son of a lowly Sheikh to one of the richest men on earth, Zayed remains a remarkeable example of what one can achieve with a bit of luck and a lot of tenacity. More importantly, Zayed was an archetypal benign monarch, and people such as him are constant examples espoused by supporters of monarchies across the world. Despite his almost unchallenged power, Zayed remained open until his death and defended personal liberty relentlessly. When asked about democracy in a 1997 interview with the New York times, Zayed argued that one did not need democracy to grant power to the people, merely the belief "that Allah has created people free, and has prescribed that each individual must enjoy freedom of choice. No one should act as if they own others." and the willpower to act upon it.
Welcome, oh Sheikh, the world is richer for your presence. You began your reign as the lowly Emir of a single emirate - barely a few thousand people on the edge of the brutal Arabian desert. Under your tutelage the harsh region soon blossomed into a garden of delights scarcely imagineable by your forebearers. In 1971 you led your people to independence and unified the seven emirates of Trucial Oman into the UAE, and within decades the federation had grown into a regional power. All over the world, the mere mention of your megacities conjure up visions of riches beyond the wildest dreams of the most ambitious dreamer. You grew the UAE into one of the richest places on earth, and opened the harsh desert to the world, where it became a global centre for tourism, business and the arts. Under the tutelage of you and your fellow monarchs, some of the greatest wonders of the 21st century were constructed - the tallest towers, the most opulent hotels and the most beautiful palaces. [NEWLINE][NEWLINE] Sheikh, the people of the gulf now look to you to bring them gold, silver and diamonds galore. Will you make the UAE into a a hub for the rich and famous - a land of wealth and oppurtunity? Will you turn your megacities into the shining pearls they should be, glistening in the Arab sun? Can you build a civilisation to stand the test of time?

Sultanate of Oman
History
The Sultanate of Oman is a nation based in the South-East corner of the Arabian Peninsula. It has a large costal region, where the majority of the population reside, as well as a mostly desert interior. Oman has two enclaves to its north, based around the United Arab Emirates, known as Madha and Musandam. The present day capital of Oman is at Muscat, and has been for many years previously, even at the time of the much larger empire. For many years, Oman was controlled by powers outside their lands, and only with the rise of Islam did the nation truly prosper. Oman managed to establish a trans-continental empire with acquisitions in Africa, and with growing presence around the Arabian Peninsula it became a vital trading spot. However, the Sultanate fell into decline during the 19th century, and after stagnating for several years, it managed to get itself back up on its feet during the second half of the 20th century; Oman survives to this day, even retaining its ancient Sultan.
Geography and Climate
Though Oman has a large amount of coastal area, it is mainly desert, thus rendering many places uninhabitable. Most cities are built near to the coast, as a result of many years of ensuring water supplies. Oman was mostly covered in water in the past; we know this due a large in-land amount of fossils. Oman receives very little precipitation, and the interior of the country is very warm and dry as a result, with little to no cooling from ocean currents. The coastal areas tend to have a better living climate; while still very warm, they are also quite humid. However, the mountainous areas of Oman get slightly more rainfall than other parts, due to the monsoon season, and as a result, they have a more tropical climate, as compared to the desert plains of the rest of the country. The Omani Sultanate also expanded into Africa and Yemen; the former having an almost exclusively costal part reserved for the Sultanate, while still very warm due to its position at the equator, and the latter is similar to Oman itself.
Prehistory
Oman’s first signs of civilisation begin with a site in the Dhofar region of the country, the most westward part of the nation; the site that commences Oman’s rich history is the Nubian Complex. Though the artefacts found there were similar to others already found, it was the first in the south of the Arabian Peninsula. The site is estimated to be around 106,000 years old, and as a result, it is used as a base to assign a date to the human migration from Africa to Arabia. The oldest inhabited site in Oman is known as Dereaze; located in the modern day city of Ibri, it dates back around eight thousand years. Nearby, cave paintings have also been discovered. Over all the sites, items such as pottery and spears were discovered. All this evidence shows that Oman’s history is truly ancient, with the Sultanate itself only forming a very small part of its rich and vibrant history.
Before Oman
In Sumer, to the north of present-day Oman, tablets had the name “Magan” or “Makan” written on them. This was a name used to refer to the copper mines in present-day Oman; so essentially Oman’s birth certificate. The present-day name of Oman is believed to have originated from around the same time, coming from Arab tribes who emigrated there from Yemen. A lot of these tribes decided to stick to the coastal regions of Oman, making a livelihood out of fishing or farming. For years afterwards, the classical world came to Oman, with three Persian Dynasties presiding over it until about the 7th century AD. Though Oman had little to no recognition as a state during this time, it was about to get it, no matter if the world was prepared for it or not. In 620, a monuments event happened that changed the course of world history, and perhaps more so than many, the history of Oman – the founding of Islam in Mecca.[NEWLINE][NEWLINE]As the Omanis were among the first to adopt the religion, they were also among the first to begin their own Islamic empire – for the first time in history, the Omanis were recognised as a separate culture from the Persians or anyone else who once dominated them – casting off their chains, they set out to create an empire.
Rise of Islam
'Amr ibn al-'As, a contemporary of Muhammad, is normally credited with converting the Omanis to Islam. Around 630 AD, he was given the task of converting the co-rulers of Oman at the time, Jayfar and ‘Abd to Islam – he succeeded in his task. In doing so, Oman’s systems of governance changed to fit in with their sect of Islam, the Ibadi – the ruler became an Imam, an elected governor of the nation. Soon after the world was rocked with Islam came the death of the prophet Muhammad, and soon after, the struggle for power over the Islamic faith. This eventually split Islam over the leader of their faith, and Oman played a major role in this. However, it also took the time to develop its economic situation, and managed to elevate itself to become a major trader in the region, and as a result, managed to gain immense wealth and control. The leadership struggle in Oman was far from over, though; within five hundred years, Oman had managed to have five dynasties in command, mostly outsiders. However, this relentless power struggle made for some ambition of an Omani state, as with no one government in command, who were they to get to lead but themselves? Come several battles with other outsiders, they did just that.
Portuguese Invasion
Vasco de Gama, a Portuguese explorer, visited the Far East close to the advent of the 16th century. Impressed by Gama’s success in trade there, later Portuguese explorers went on to capture the present-day Omani capital of Muscat. The Portuguese built up defence in the city, though it was captured by the Ottoman Empire in 1552, during their fight for supremacy in India and the Persian Gulf. The Ottomans again recaptured Muscat in 1581, and held it until the following year. During this time, neither the Portuguese nor the Ottomans managed to take all of Oman; no outside power has ever done so. The Portuguese were thrown out of Oman in the 17th century, and were usurped by native Omani tribes; however, this did not last long, as Yemeni tribes managed to take over Oman around a century later. Though this may not sound like much, this is the dynasty that went on to take over Oman. Though the Persians briefly recaptured parts of Oman after the Yemeni takeover, Oman has been independent ever since.
Foundations of the Sultanate
With the coming of a suitable leader came the beginnings of an empire. Saif bin Sultan, possibly the greatest leader of Oman, became Imam (Omani leader) in 1692. To expand Oman’s sphere of influence and the empire, Saif focused on a takeover of the west coast of Africa, beginning with the remaining Portuguese settlements. Fort Jesus, a Portuguese stronghold in Africa, was among the main obstacles in Saif’s imperial plans. Saif took up arms to fight for the fort; come 1698, Saif’s famous Siege of Fort Jesus proved successful, and the beginning of a mighty trading empire commenced.[NEWLINE][NEWLINE]The Sultanate went on to siege and conquer the rest of Portuguese possessions in East Africa. They were rulled in a manner similar to the Portuguese hold on Muscat; though Oman had a firm grip on the cities themselves, they ruled very little of the nearby land, and most of what they claimed could not really be said to be controlled by them. The Persians, however, managed to siege Oman for around a decade starting in 1737. The saviours of the Omani Empire were the Al Said dynasty, who managed to recapture Oman along with all colonial positions from the Persians, and they still rule to this day.
Height of the Empire
Out of all the positions Oman had managed to attain over the years, Zanzibar was among the most precious. The ever-growing Slave market was to some extent centred there, and to show its importance, Imam Said bin Sultan built his main palace there, and ruled over the empire from its colonies, for the most part, doing so after the capture of Mombasa, further expanding his African Empire. Said’s rule marked the height of the empire, when Oman was thriving and in few difficulties. Said managed to sort out trading relations with the United States of America with very good terms for Oman, and as sole ruler of the sultanate, he was able to make such decisions very easily. Said is a very well-respected Omani leader to this day, and even has a museum dedicated to his possession.[NEWLINE][NEWLINE]After Said died, there was a succession crisis between his two sons, which was settled by the British; the territory of Oman was split between the two in such a way that one got the possessions in East Africa, though they were soon reclaimed by the Portuguese, and the other got control of the Omani homelands, at the time, Muscat and Oman. The latter territory was very much under British influence, though it was not a colonial possession of the British Empire by any stretch. Instead, it was a powerful trading link to their Indian and other Asian colonies, making the alliance with Oman evermore important for Britain. This act of division pretty much ended the two and a half centuries of Omani dominance in the region; it was divided between several lesser entities, and a few greater ones.
Muscat and Oman
The present-day nation of Oman was once divided into two distinct regions, namely Muscat and Oman. The former referred to the city of Muscat, now the nation’s capital, as well as other coastal areas of the nation. The term Oman was more to do with the desert interior of the country. This distinction was important in terms of governance; Oman was ruled by a Sultan, while the Imam retained control over Muscat. This was the result of several disagreements over the control of Oman, and was mostly planned by the British. While Muscat and Oman was never actually a British colony, it is safe to say that Britain certainly had a lot of influence and authority over it.[NEWLINE][NEWLINE]Muscat and Oman functioned as a single political entity, and did so during its 150 years of establishment. During the reign of Sultan Said bin Taimur, Muscat and Oman was able to become richer, strengthening the nation and putting in the foundations for the country today. With control over Muscat came a larger amount of power over external treaties; Oman was far more concerned with internal issues. When the oil market opened up in the Middle East, and Iraqi oil company was interested in dealing with Muscat and Oman. This lead to a dispute between Sultan Said and the Imam of Oman, Ghalib Al Hinai, over who should have final say over the oil. Said claimed the oil as external deals came under his area of influence, while Ghalib claimed it due to his control over the land the oil was on. Said went on to invade Oman, and took key oil sites, though never fully occupied the entire nation given that they were already unified by law.[NEWLINE][NEWLINE]Said also managed to secure deals with Pakistan over the territories of Makran and Gwadar, Omani enclaves in Pakistan – the latter was sold for three million dollars. Doing so made Oman richer, and along with their oil deals, they were able to progress at a far faster rate. However, due to the divisive nature of Muscat and Oman, it was far harder to say who should get power over what. In 1965, a rebellion occurred in Dhofar over exploitation from the Sultan. It was clear that Said was not doing all he could to meet the demands of his people; there was always a serious threat of overthrow for him, and in 1970, the coup happened – though lead by his own son.
Oman Today
Sultan Qaboos seized power in 1970, and began to reform the country very quickly, dragging it out from being one of the worse-off nations of the Middle East. He opened up the nation to outside powers, enriching it in the process. With more money being put into healthcare, education and welfare, the Omani people were far better off, and ready to write the next chapter in Omani history. Through years of political reform, women were given the right to vote, a massive step forwards in the development of rights. However, there is some dispute over whether or not this means much; voting is said to be somewhat useless, as the elected representatives have little to no power, as all real authority lies with the Sultan.[NEWLINE][NEWLINE]As a result, the Sultanate still suffers from many problems, given the Sultan’s authoritarian ruling style. Oman was affected by the Arab Spring, as protesters took to the streets to speak out against the political system, and to tell the world about the lack of jobs there. Qaboos promised further political reform, though as of May 2014, it has not yet been delivered, despite the pledge being almost four years ago. Despite all these problems, Oman’s economic situation is improving vastly, and the nation as a whole is doing very well on the world stage.
Oman Factoids
Oman has retained political ties with the United Kingdom and the United States almost since the establishment of them.[NEWLINE][NEWLINE]Due to Sultan Qaboos’ reforms, Oman ranked as the most developed country in the world, according to the United Nations Development Program.[NEWLINE][NEWLINE]The symbol of Oman, known as a Khanjar, is actually a type of dagger. It is featured on both their Coat of Arms and their flag.
Saif bin Sultan
c. 160 - 1711
Saif bin Sultan
Imam of Oman
Imam
History
The Imam of the Omani Sultanate, Saif bin Sultan, was instrumental in the process of assuring that Oman was a dominant power in the region. By taking control of Portuguese possessions in East Africa, he made the empire span two continents, thus putting it in an ever more vital trading position. Saif is credited as one of the greatest Omani leaders, a well-deserved title after doing so much to make sure that Oman would prosper in the region for centuries to come. Oman held the East African possessions until a leadership dispute in the 19th century, and given he preceded these arguments by more than two hundred years, it is safe to say that his efforts were worth it, as he managed to create an Omani national identity, as well as ensuring that Oman was safe from outside invasion, a promise broken only once by flawed leadership soon after his death.
Early Life
Saif bin Sultan was born in the 17th century, not long after Oman had managed to gain independence from any outsiders. Saif was the second son of his father, and as a result, did not become the Imam of Oman immediately. Saif’s father, Sultan bin Saif, died in 1679. Bil’arab bin Sultan, the brother of Saif, took control of the country after his father’s death; Saif seemed happy with being second-in-command to his brother. However, his happiness with Bil’arab’s reign was cut short by a dispute between the brothers, and soon enough, Saif built up a force to go after him, and managed to hold up Bil’arab in his fort in Jabrin until 1692, when he died. Given that Saif was next in line to the Omani throne, as well as the dominant power in Oman, it was all but obvious that he should succeed. The same year, Saif became the fourth Imam of Oman, and possibly the greatest as well.
Imam of Oman
Early on in his reign, the Sultan focused on improving the infrastructure of Oman. With the advent of his reign, water supplies were focused on along with improvements to farming, making irrigation easier. Saif put Date Palm Trees near the coastal areas of Oman to encourage the desert dwellers, the Arabs in particular, to live nearer the coast. In line with the tradition of Omani leaders having a primary adobe, Saif chose to stay in Rustaq for the majority of the time, and added a new wind tower there early in his reign. The fort at Rustaq had been there several centuries prior to Islam’s founding; however, improvements by Saif, notably the walls built in 1711, made the fort even harder to break in the event of siege, and are said to be a fantastic example of Islamic architecture. Nearby the fort lies several other improvements that Saif made possible, such as large agricultural and irrigation areas.
The Seige of Fort Jesus
Aiming to get back at the Portuguese invaders, Saif bin Sultan struck back hard at the Siege of Fort Jesus. In 1696, Saif had attacked Mombasa in an attempt to take it from the Portuguese, though they had retreated to Fort Jesus nearby. Though Oman had managed to attack Mombasa several times, almost breaking it in 1660, they had yet to take a Portuguese possession fully. Almost immediately after the Portuguese retreat, Saif put pressure down on the Portuguese positions in Fort Jesus, and sieged it for almost 33 months. So brutal was the siege that of the 2,500 people who took refuge in the fort when Oman attacked, only 13 were alive at the end of the siege in 1698.[NEWLINE][NEWLINE]The fort was held by around seventy Portuguese soldiers, and most of the civilians there were Arabs. Though the Queen of Zanzibar managed to get supplies through to the fort to keep up the health of the garrison, the Portuguese, immensely more powerful and with more to supply to the garrison, failed to provide anything. The siege was lifted at the end of 1696, when the Portuguese managed to get their first supplies in. However, Oman returned to the fort, and kept the pressure up until all of the Portuguese soldiers were killed due to disease. For around six to nine months, the defence of the fort was left in the hands of some of the native Africans, led by Sheikh Daud of Faza, leading eight men and fifty women, along with seventeen members of family – not an ideal fighting force. In late 1697, Portugal managed to get a few more reinforcements in, though these measures proved to be too little. On December the 13th 1698, Oman managed to capture the fort. A few days later, a Portuguese ship arrived to resupply the garrison, though it arrived too late. Oman had won; this victory secured their possession of Mombasa for nearly thirty years, and served as a harbinger to their dominance of the East African coast.
Attacks on the Portuguese
After the monumental success in Mombasa, the Omani forces went on to take several other key Portuguese positions within a few months. Pemba Island, Kilwa and Zanzibar quickly fell to Oman, and before long, they dominated East Africa, as the once-mighty Portuguese presence there had been dwarfed by the power of Oman’s navy. This gained Saif quite some reputation for doing such attacks; he was given the nickname the “Chain of the Earth” for the attacks he had managed to carry out on the Portuguese possessions. To show his dominance in the region, he encouraged large-scale repopulations of newly captured territory such as Zanzibar and Mombasa, thus making sure that Omani presence was felt, asserting his authority across all territories he called his. Saif managed to gain a vast amount of wealth from his general assets, and to ensure that Oman remained the dominant economic power in the region, he advocated piracy against other nation’s ships. This made sure that they could not compete with Oman’s vast trading network, and overall, it helped Oman for the better.
Later Reign
During the latter half of Saif bun Sultan’s reign, Oman didn’t expand much more, rather focus on improving what they had. This allowed for Saif to become vastly wealthier than he was at the start of his reign, overall improving Oman’s economy for the better. Saif also helped to open up the Slave Trade for Oman, and while highly questionable about whether it was morally correct or not, it was no doubt a large source of income for them. Saif died in 1711, and while the prosperity of his reign did not instantly fade, his political skills were not matched by his successors. Saif was noted for being incredibly wealthy at the end of his reign, with assets including 700 male slaves, 28 ships and a third of Oman’s palm trees, which were a large source of income at the time. With a comfortable burial at his fort of Rustaq later that year, the magnificence of the Imam’s reign ended.
Judgement of History
Saif was renowned for his skill to avoid internal troubles, and instead focusing people’s anger on others, all part of why he advocated piracy. Doing so made sure that he had a far more stable empire with people willing to defend it, and even defending it on a day-to-day basis without even noticing. By avoiding all internal troubles, he was able to make far more money off the country than many could even hope to attain, and with his love of money and power, he was able to rule the empire in an incredibly authoritarian yet efficient way. Today, Saif is revered as a national hero, and has created a legacy of bringing Portugal to breaking point and improving Oman’s fortunes, in effect, creating an identity for them.
Saif bin Sultan Factoids
Saif bin Sultan was a member of the Ibadi sect of Islam, the sect originally introduced to Oman when Islam came to the nation.[NEWLINE][NEWLINE]Samuel Barrett Miles, a British Officer and Diplomat who served in Oman, said this of Saif: “The Imam Saif bin Sultan was the greatest of the Yaareba Princes, and at no time before or since has Oman been so renowned, powerful or prosperous as under his sway…”

The Panama Canal is a manmade shipping lane located on the Panama Isthmus seperating the Pacific Ocean and Carribean Sea. The idea of a canal in the location was first proposed int he sixteenth century by Charles V, Holy Roman Emperor, who asked for a link to shorten the journey between Spain and their colony of Peru. In 1698 the Kingdom of Scotland launched a project to create an overland trade route in the area, which was abandoned due to inhospitiable conditions a year later. It was not until 1855 that a link was first established, the Panama Canal Railway, as a result of the 1849 discovery of Gold in the American state of California. This railway was used extensively in the American construction of the canal from 1904 to 1914. As opposed to the French plan of constructing a flat water canal, much like that of the Suez Canal, the American design featured a series of ship locks to rise the ships over a range that caused problems for the French design. The American design proved sucessful, and was opened on August 15, 1914. Railway cars had been used to transport approximately 152,910,972 cubic metres of excevations through the construction, while it had cost 27,500 lives across the whole project.

Cuba
History
Cuba is the largest Caribbean island. It was once inhabited by the Taino, or Arawak people, among others. Since its colonization in the 15th century by the Spanish, Cuba has been a key part of the New World colonies and a key strategic place in the Caribbean. Its prominence in the region, its economy and its proximity to the territorial United States have made it a prominent colonial and postcolonial nation through the Age of Discovery, the Latin American independence struggle, and the Cold War.
Geography and Climate
Cuba is the largest island in the Caribbean, and the 17th largest in the world. Cuba’s narrow landmass spans a large swath of the Gulf of Mexico. Its climate is tropical, which tailors the environment to the cultivation of sugar cane and its byproducts. This tropical climate subjects Cuba to year-round warm weather, but also the danger of Atlantic hurricanes.
Colonial History
Cuba was a Spanish colony for centuries, from the late 1400s to 1898. Christophor Colombus arrived with his three ships in 1492. Twenty years later, Spanish settlements began to pop up. Unlike other Caribbean colonies, over the centuries Cuba became quite urbanized, and had a diversified economy. Cuba had a substantial slave population. Cuban planters benefitted from the successful slave revolt in Haiti, in that they were able to anticipate similar unrest in Cuba. While this helped to perpetuate the institution of slavery in the colony and indeed the colonial rule itself, 19th Century Cuba had a significantly higher amount of free persons of color than other slaveholding states at the time.
Independent Cuba
Cuba’s independence took much longer than other Latin American nations.In the second half of the 1800s, about forty years after all other Latin American nations began to become independent, Cuban planter Carlos Manuel de Cespedes launched an uprising known as the Ten Years War, which did not end in independence, but did win the Cubans a promise of greater autonomy from Spain. Slavery was abolished in 1875. Cuba finally won its independence in 1898, with the help of exiled dissident Jose Marti, a writer who penned his Manifesto of Montecristi before his death in a battle in 1895. Marti is regarded as Cuba’s national hero. The Americans became involved in the conflict when their battleship, the Maine, exploded in the harbor in Havana. American journalist William Randolph Hearst’s (who supported the Cuban rebels) sensationalist coverage of the incident helped to bring the conflict to a head in the Spanish-American War, which ended in the 1898 Treaty of Paris, granting Cuba its independence after four centuries.
The Revolution
The first few decades of Cuban independence were rather prosperous, but prosperity was confined to the wealthy. Especially during the rule of Fulgencio Batista, Cuba was known for its tourism industry – both Frank Sinatra and the American Mafia were influential in Havana in the 1950s. Cuba was relatively well-developed for the region, thanks to its more urban organization. The Cuban Revolution took place in 1959. Fidel Castro, a militant student activist in the 1940s, attempted to start a violent revolution through his organization MR 26-7. After a failed attack on Moncada Barracks, Castro was imprisoned but eventually pardoned. Fleeing to Mexico, Castro fell in with Argentine Marxist Che Guevara. Together, Castro and Guevara recruited allies and trained on guerrilla warfare. The pair, along Castro’s brother Raul and Camilo Cienfuegos, returned to Cuba in the mid 1950s. Engaging in guerrilla warfare, MR 26-7 engaged in agitation in the cities while Castro’s group recruited local peasants and raided army bases in the jungles and mountains. Batista’s regime crumbled under a faltering military and collapsing public support. An American-backed right-wing coup deposed him – but the junta was itself deposed in 1959, when Castro and Guevara took Havana.
Cuba and Soviet Russia
During the Cold War, Cuba, as America’s closest Communist neighbor, needed to align themselves with the Soviet Union in order to survive economically and politically. Castro was subjected to a number of assassination attempts by the CIA, including the failed support of the Bay of Pigs invasion. These tensions came to a head in the Cuban Missile Crisis in 1962. Cuba had requested the placement of Soviet nuclear missiles in Cuba to prevent future harassment from the Americans. Soviet premier Nikita Khrushchev agreed, as the Americans had upset the thermonuclear balance by placing missiles in Turkey. American spy planes discovered the transport of these missiles, and blockaded further importation of missiles. After two weeks of tense negotiation, the Soviet missiles were pulled back, as were the American counterparts in Turkey. This crisis had far-reaching implications for the ongoing Cold War, but Cuba was merely a place for these events to occur, rather than a meaningful actor. Fidel Castro was not at the negotiating table during the crisis. While Cuba was still aligned with the Soviets politically and economically, Castro turned to the Non-Aligned Movement during the next few decades.
The Special Period
After the end of the Cold War, Cuba lost much of its Communist trade due to the dissolution of the Soviet Union. The severe economic depression persisted throughout the 1990s, and was most evident in a massive shortage of gasoline and fuel. Famine led to rationing, which persists to this day. The Cuban economy began to recover late in the decade – one source of help was a new alignment with left-wing Latin American states like Venezuela and Bolivia.
Cuba after Fidel
Fidel Castro turned over presidential duties to his brother Raul in 2006, citing health concerns. In recent years, Cuba and the Untied States have warmed relations. In 2015, embassies reopened in Havana and Washington, and travel and trade restrictions began to ease. Despite this, Cuba remains a steadfast Communist nation 25 years after the end of the Soviet Union. Cuba remains an important Latin American political actor, with Miami’s substantial Cuban refugee population continuing their resistance to the Castros from afar.
Trivia
-Fidel Castro attended El Colegio de Belen, a Jesuit-run predatory school, in 1945. After Communist Cuba expelled the Jesuits, the school relocated to Miami, where it still operates today. -During the Ten Years War, two thousand Chinese indentured servants fought on the side of the rebels. Today, there is a monument in their honor in Havana. -In 2000, a statue of John Lennon was built in Havana. The Beatles were banned in the 1960s and 70s. -Cuba’s literacy rate of 99.7% is one of the highest in the world. 1961, just after the revolution, was dedicated to education through the Cuban Literacy Campaign.

Guerrilla war in Cuba was very different to that conducted elsewhere in the world for one primary reason: the concept of “foquismo”. Codified into a proper political theory by Régis Debray after the Cuban Revolution, it centred on the idea that a small paramilitary force could provide a focal point for a popular uprising, which ran counter to the accepted doctrine among revolutionaries that one had to wait for the popular struggle before one could begin the armed struggle. This was inspired by the Maoist idea of “people’s war”, but was unique to Cuba’s revolutionaries - and its use elsewhere to aid the struggles of Marxist rebellions led directly to the death of Che Guevara in Bolivia.

Dance Hall
Cuba’s tradition of popular music began with musical theatre and the “zarzuela” operetta form, a light, satirical opera originally from Spain that turned into a kind of running commentary on Cuban current events. This gave rise to the “bufo” style of musical comedy, which itself spawned the still-practiced guaracha movement. However, the biggest and most important aspect of Cuban music is son, which filled the dance halls and the airwaves alike with Afro-Cuban rhythms. However, the party couldn’t last; it was eventually superseded by jazz and swing, with Arsenio Rodriguez and Beny More the last of the great son artists. It lost its controversial edge, and that would never do in Cuba.

Fidel Castro

Fidel Castro
Leader of Cuba
Prime Minister of Cuba (1959-1973)
President of Cuba (1973-2008)
First Secretary of the Cuban Communist Party (1961-2011)
History
Fidel Castro was the head of state of Cuba from the success of its Communist revolution to his retirement due to age and declining health in 2008. Castro headed one of the longest-lasting Communist governments in history, that still persists to this day. Communist Cuba remains critical in North American geopolitics, maintaining an icy relationship with the United States even after the Cold War ended, due in part to brinksmanship between America and Castro’s Cuba.
Early Life
Castro was the son of a wealthy sugar cane farmer, an immigrant from Galicia. Sent to Catholic school at a young age, Castro did not become interested in politics until he began studying law at the University of Havana. There, he began his involvement with leftist and anti-imperialist politics. After a number of unsuccessful attempts at political activism, including running for the presidency of his school’s student federation, his politics became increasingly radical. As student activism became more violent, so did Castro. He participated in a number of ventures across Latin America, including a failed coup attempt in the Dominican Republic. As he began his family, he returned to a more peaceful, but still activist, career in law. However, the coup by right-wing politician Fulgencio Batista drove Fidel Castro to revulsion,
MR 26-7
Castro and many other Cubans decided to fight what they perceived to be Batista’s tyranny. Castro took direct action, founding a paramilitary called “The Movement.”The first major action by The Movement was to attack Moncada Barracks, in Santiago de Cuba. The attack proved disastrous.Fidel and his brother Raul led 135 revolutionaries – 61 were killed and 51 captured. Castro himself was tried and sentenced to 15 years in prison, but not before giving a famous speech, where he justified his actions and stated that “history will absolve me. A few years later, Batista pardoned Castro, beliving him to no longer be a threat. This was not the case. “The Movement’ became the “July 26th Movement”, or MR-26-7. While MR 26-7 cells prepared for a bigger action, Castro fled to Mexico with his brother, where he fell in with Argentine communist fighter Che Guevara. In Mexico, and with Guevara’s and others’ help, Castro and his associates trained in clandestine and guerrilla warfare, the kind they needed to take the fight to Batista.
Return to Cuba
Castro and company returned to Cuba by boat in December of 1956. Only a small group of about 20 were able to encamp in the jungle. Castro’s group began raiding army outposts for supplies and weapons. They were aided by Guevara’s training as a doctor, along with support and trust from the locals. 26-7 cells continued their campaign of agitation while sending Castro supplies. Castro’s strategy worked. His tactics endeared him to locals, allowing him to constantly grow his forces. Escalation meant that Batista’s soldiers turned even more brutal, causing further public outrage against his government. In 1959, Castro’s forces took Havana from a military junta that had been established (with American backing) to displace the failing Batista. He was sworn in as Prime Minister in February of that year.
Cuba under Castro
Castro’s Cuba did not start off as explicitly socialist as he is remembered – however, his regime certainly developed into a socialist state, popular with workers and peasants but unpopular among the intelligentsia, many of whom emigrated (legally or otherwise) to the United States and elsewhere. Cuba was closely associated with the Soviet Union and global communism during the Cold War. Famously, the United States sponsored the Bay of Pigs invasion, a guerrilla force that was designed to remove Castro from power in 1961. It proved disastrous. Cuba was also central to the Cuban Missile Crisis, whereupon Soviet premier Nikita Khrushchev planned to install a Soviet missile base in Cuba, infuriating the nearby Americans. This incident was perhaps the closest the world has come to global nuclear war. Cuba was used as battleground, but had no place in the negotiations, infuriating Castro. After the Cuban Missile Crisis, Castro has turned more toward the Non-Aligned Movement for political support, even serving as President. Cuba was still committed to socialism, though – it directly supported Angola’s Marxist MPLA at the request of Agostinho Neto in the 1970s. Castro’s Cuba survived the end of the Cold War, although not unscathed. The Special Period, during the 1990s, was a period of economic hardship brought on by the loss of Communist trading partners. Cuba somewhat regained its footing in the 2000s, by aligning itself with leftist governments in South America, like Hugo Chavez’ Venezuela. Castro began to fall into ill health in the 2000s, turning over his presidential duties to his brother Raul in 2006. Raul was formally elected in 2008.
Judgement of History
Castro is viewed negatively by many in the West, especially the United States. His role in the Cuban Missile Crisis, along with the substantial (and politically active) Cuban-American population has made the Cold War last longer politically than historically, when it comes to relations between the two countries. However, in 2015, America and Cuba finally reestablished embassies. Castro’s rule was not economically successful, but its longevity, persisting at least 25 years after the end of the Cold War, is notable. Communist Cuba has also been widely criticized for its human rights violations.

Bolivia
History
Bolivia, officially the Plurinational State of Bolivia, is a landlocked country located in western-central South America. The capital is Sucre while the seat of government is located in La Paz. The largest city and principal economic and financial center is Santa Cruz de la Sierra, located on the Llanos Orientales (tropical lowlands) a mostly flat region in the east of Bolivia.[NEWLINE][NEWLINE]It is constitutionally a unitary state, divided into nine departments. Its geography varies from the peaks of the Andes in the West, to the Eastern Lowlands, situated within the Amazon Basin. It is bordered to the north and east by Brazil, to the southeast by Paraguay, to the south by Argentina, to the southwest by Chile, and to the northwest by Peru. One-third of the country is within the Andean mountain range. With 1,098,581 km2 (424,164 sq mi) of area, Bolivia is the 5th largest country in South America and the 27th largest in the world.[NEWLINE][NEWLINE]The country's population, estimated at 11 million, is multiethnic, including Amerindians, Mestizos, Europeans, Asians and Africans. The racial and social segregation that arose from Spanish colonialism has continued to the modern era. Spanish is the official and predominant language, although 36 indigenous languages also have official status, of which the most commonly spoken are Guarani, Aymara and Quechua languages.[NEWLINE][NEWLINE]Before Spanish colonization, the Andean region of Bolivia was part of the Inca Empire, while the northern and eastern lowlands were inhabited by independent tribes. Spanish conquistadors arriving from Cuzco and Asunción took control of the region in the 16th century. During the Spanish colonial period Bolivia was administered by the Royal Audiencia of Charcas. Spain built its empire in great part upon the silver that was extracted from Bolivia's mines. After the first call for independence in 1809, 16 years of war followed before the establishment of the Republic, named for Simón Bolívar. Over the course of the 19th and early 20th century Bolivia lost control of several peripheral territories to neighboring countries including the seizure of its coastline by Chile in 1879. Bolivia remained relatively politically stable until 1971, when Hugo Banzer led a coup d'état which replaced the socialist government of Juan José Torres with a military dictatorship headed by Banzer; Torres was murdered in Buenos Aires, Argentina by a right-wing death squad in 1976. Banzer's regime cracked down on leftist and socialist opposition and other forms of dissent, resulting in the torture and deaths of a number of Bolivian citizens. Banzer was ousted in 1978 and later returned as the democratically elected president of Bolivia from 1997 to 2001.[NEWLINE][NEWLINE]Modern Bolivia is a charter member of the UN, IMF, NAM, OAS, ACTO, Bank of the South, ALBA and USAN. For over a decade Bolivia has had one of the fastest economic growths in Latin America, however it remains one of the poorest countries in South America. It is a developing country, with a medium ranking in the Human Development Index, a poverty level of 38.6 percent, and it has one of the lowest crime rates in Latin America. Its main economic activities include agriculture, forestry, fishing, mining, and manufacturing goods such as textiles, clothing, refined metals, and refined petroleum. Bolivia is very rich in minerals, especially tin.

Manuel Belzu
History
Manuel Isidoro Belzu Humerez was president of Bolivia from 1848 to 1855. Born in La Paz, Bolivia to humble mestizo parents, Belzu was educated by Franciscan friars. He joined the wars of independence in his youth, fighting under Andres de Santa Cruz at Zepita (1823) when he was 17. After serving as an aide to Agustin Gamarra, he left the Peruvian army when the latter entered Bolivia in 1828. Assigned as garrison commander to Tarija, Belzu married "up" in class by wedding a beautiful and intellectual Argentine lady, Juana Manuela Gorriti, who resided there with her family.[NEWLINE][NEWLINE]Belzu fought in the battles of the Peru-Bolivian Confederacy, during which he was promoted to the post of Army commander by President Jose Ballivian. He had fought bravely under his orders at the Battle of Ingavi (1841).[NEWLINE][NEWLINE]Originally a close friend and supporter of President Ballivian, Belzu turned against him about 1845. Ballivian had reportedly attempted to seduce Belzu's wife in his own Oruro home. Surprising the President there, Belzu shot at him and barely missed. The event sealed an undying enmity between the two that would never abate. Political ambitions—typical of upper-level Bolivian military officers at the time—may have played a role in addition to the personal reasons. Belzu decided at that point to try to topple the "Hero of Ingavi" from the presidency. Withdrawing to the countryside (orders for his arrest for the attempted murder of the President had been issued), Belzu never ceased to conspire against his former friend.[NEWLINE][NEWLINE]Belzu's political stance became more populist as he embraced his mestizo heritage, railed against the power of the "white" oligarchy, and vowed to advance the cause of the poor and the Indian should he come to the presidency. In his travels as a fugitive, Belzu had seen the deplorable conditions under which most of the population lived, with scarcely any improvements or public works by the government. His position established a strong base of support among the peasants, who came to know him as "Tata (Father, or Protector) Belzu."[NEWLINE][NEWLINE]Another, more conventional anti-Ballivian insurgent group was commanded by the ambitious former president, Jose Miguel de Velasco. As a warlord, he led his army in competition with that of Belzu in the race to topple the President. The embattled Ballivian found the country ungovernable, and in December 1847 he fled to exile abroad. He left the government in the hands of General Eusebio Guilarte, head of the Council of State and legally second-in-line to the presidency.[NEWLINE][NEWLINE]At this point Belzu made a pact with Velasco to support the latter's accession to the Presidency while Belzu took the position of Minister of War. Belzu quickly betrayed Velasco and had his troops proclaim him as President. A bloody counter-coup by General Velasco had to be put down, with Belzu's commanding the troops that crushed Velasco's. By the end of the year, Belzu had destroyed the opposition (both Ballivian and Velasco) and consolidated his power as the sole de facto president of Bolivia.[NEWLINE][NEWLINE]As promised, Belzu led his government in undertaking populist measures, but he also wanted to maintain strong control over power. Most of Belzu's reforms were cosmetic, although his political statements were more liberal than any president's had been since Sucre. capitalizing on his relative popularity, Belzu managed to legitimize his rule by becoming democratically elected. He faced constant opposition and rebellions from the pro-Ballivian camp, from ambitious fellow military warlords, and later, from the pro-Linares faction that coalesced as a united front against military caudillism. Belzu's protectionist economic policies were opposed by Great Britain and the United States, and isolated Bolivia from the global economy and ongoing intellectual trends. Although popular with the masses due to his statist policies (contrary to prevailing notions), Belzu never lacked enemies among the powerful, whose interests he threatened. He barely survived a well-planned assassination attempt in Sucre, carried out by Agustin Morales, then an obscure mid-ranking officer but one who would later become president.[NEWLINE][NEWLINE]By the early 1850s, Belzu dispensed with any pretense of democratic norms and ruled despotically. Following a prolonged, 7-year rule, in 1855 a weary Belzu decided to "retire". He ran elections in which he sponsored the candidacy of his loyal son-in-law, General Jorge Cordova. The latter was duly elected over Jose Maria Linares (perhaps with the help of at least some degree of official fraud), and for two years ruled Bolivia as a virtual proxy of the powerful former president. During this time, Belzu served as his country's Plenipotentiary in Europe.[NEWLINE][NEWLINE]Cordova was overthrown in an 1857 coup d'etat. Still acting as Belzu's proxy, he was murdered after being caught plotting against President Jose Maria de Acha in 1862. This galvanized Belzu despite his age, who returned to Bolivia and raised an army, with the hope of returning to the presidency and avenging the death of his son-in-law. Never flagging in his campaign, Belzu came close to becoming President for a second time in 1864 when Acha finally fled Bolivia. Another general, Mariano Melgarejo, preceded Belzu's forces to the government palace of La Paz, by then the country's largest city and the defacto seat of government. Belzu tried to besiege the city, but Melgarejo, also a mestizo, became as popular as the "Tata."[NEWLINE][NEWLINE]Purportedly to avoid bloodshed, Melgarejo sent an emissary to Belzu, and invited him to the Government Palace to make a pact to share power in his administration. He reportedly offered to cede power to the former President in exchange for some concessions. Trusting Melgarejo, Belzu arrived at the Palace and was assassinated in January 1865 on its grounds, presumably at the hands of the new dictator and caudillo.

Cardoen
In early 1990, Industrias Cardoen was on the verge of closing a deal to supply Iraq with kits for converting American-made Bell helicopters into gunships. On the afternoon of March 1, 1990, a maid entered Moyle's hotel room in Santiago and noticed the closet door was slightly ajar. Inside, she found Moyle's naked body hanging from a shirt tied round his neck, his head covered in a pillowcase and his underpants dangling round his ankles. Chilean police initially said Moyle had killed himself in a sexual ritual, but an autopsy later found a needle hole on his shin and enough tranquilizers in his stomach to knock him unconscious. Cardoen's former public-relations chief, Raul Montecinos, confessed on his deathbed in 1995 to having ordered Moyle's murder. Moyle, who also allegedly was an informant for the British Secret Service, was spooking the Iraqis with his questions about Cardoen's helicopter sales.

Cooperative
A Cooperative is an autonomous association of persons united voluntarily to meet their common economic, social, and cultural needs and aspirations through a jointly owned and democratically-controlled enterprise. Co-operatives are businesses owned and run by and for their members. Whether the members are the customers, employees or residents they have an equal say in what the business does and a share in the profits. Cooperativism in Chile was born as a product of workers and syndicalist movements. Though Cooperatives have existed in Chile since the 19th century, they didn’t really reach any significant prevalence until the creation of CORFO (Corporación Fomento Producción) where cooperativism, particularly in the agricultural sector, was greatly favored. By Allende’s presidency Cooperativism had reached its zenith in Chile, having been developed during the last government with great state support, it was partially due to this that Allende’s government decided to not touch Cooperatives during the process of nationalization of most industries. Though Cooperativism wasn’t particularly favored, they weren’t significantly hurt either. Unlike the period after the Coup, where the reorganization of the Chilean economy towards a neoliberal economy and the targeting of popular movements meant that most Cooperatives through the countries found their end.

Chile
History
Prior to the arrival of the Spanish in the 16th century, northern and central Chile was under Inca rule, while the independent Mapuche inhabited south-central Chile. Chile declared its independence from Spain on 12 February 1818. In the War of the Pacific (1879–83), Chile defeated Peru and Bolivia and won its current northern territory. It was not until the 1880s that the Mapuche were completely subjugated. In 1973 General Augusto Pinochet overthrew Chilean President Salvador Allende and instituted a 16-year-long military dictatorship (1973–90) that left more than 3,000 people dead or missing.[NEWLINE][NEWLINE]Today Chile is one of South America's most stable and prosperous nations, a recognized middle power and an emerging economy. It leads Latin American nations in human development, competitiveness, income per capita, globalization, state of peace, economic freedom, and low perception of corruption.

Bernardo O'Higgins
History
O'Higgins spent his early years with his mother's family in central-southern Chile, and later he lived with the Albano family, who were his father's commercial partners, in Talca. At age 15, O'Higgins was sent to Lima by his father. He had a distant relationship with Ambrosio, who supported him financially and was concerned with his education, but the two never met in person. It is unclear why Ambrosio did not marry Isabel. High-ranking Spanish government officials in The Americas were forbidden to marry locals, but at the time of O'Higgins' birth, Ambrosio O'Higgins was only a junior military officer. It has been suggested that Isabel's family would not have seen the match as advantageous at the time. Two years later, she married Don Felix Rodriguez, an old friend of her father's. O'Higgins used his mother's surname until the death of his father in 1801.[NEWLINE][NEWLINE]Ambrosio O'Higgins, Bernardo's father, continued his professional rise and became Viceroy of Peru; at seventeen Bernardo O'Higgins was sent to London to complete his studies. There, studying history and the arts, O'Higgins became acquainted with American ideas of independence and developed a sense of nationalist pride, coming to admire liberalism in the Georgian British model. He also met Francisco de Miranda, a Venezuelan idealist and believer in independence, and joined a Masonic Lodge established by Miranda, dedicated to achieving the independence of Latin America.[NEWLINE][NEWLINE]In 1798 O'Higgins went to Spain from England, his return to the Americas delayed by the French Revolutionary Wars. His father died in 1801, leaving O'Higgins a large piece of land, the Hacienda Las Canteras, near the Chilean city of Los Angeles. O'Higgins returned to Chile in 1802, adopted his father's surname, and began life as a gentleman farmer. In 1806 O'Higgins was appointed to the cabildo as the representative of Laja. Then, in 1808, Napoleon took control of Spain, triggering a sequence of events in South America. In Chile, the commercial and political elite decided to form an autonomous government to rule in the name of the imprisoned king Ferdinand VII; this was to be one of the first in a number of steps toward national independence, in which O'Higgins would play a leading role.

The Matato'a were the chiefs and war leaders of the mata, the large kinship groups that divided the island among themselves. Beneath them served commoners recruited for battle, armed with clubs known as paoa, from which these lowly warriors took their name. The favored weapons of the matato'a, however, were the vero and the kakau, the spear and the javelin, both tipped with vicious mataa, an obsidian point said to have been developed during the war between the hanua 'e'epe and the hanua momoko. This legendary war may be connected to the 18th Century conflicts on the island, during which mataa became increasingly common and the matato'a assumed greater control over Rapa Nui. To further secure their rule and determine which matato'a took precedence over the others, they established the competitive mata veri ceremony to chose a Tangata Manu.

While almost any Maori village could be called a pa, today the word has come to refer to fortified hilltop villages almost exclusively. Ringed with palisades and terraces, these monumental structures announced the military power of a rangatira and his iwi to the world. Pa were built in strategic places throughout an iwi’s territory, in order to best guard its fertile lands. A simple pa might consist only of a single palisade, while a more complex pa would consist of multiple rings of palisades, earthen ramparts, ditches from which to defenders can mount ambushes, kumara patches, food storage areas, wells, underground passages, and decorative entryways. During the Musket Wars, a new type of pa was developed - the gunfighter pa. These forts were usually simpler than the older varieties, but could be constructed in a matter of days. The Gunfighter pa provided greater defense against attackers wielding firearms, as well as allowing defenders to the full advantage of their own muskets.

The memory of your once vast empire still travels across the waters which once sustained it, and on the wings of the seabirds which guided its navigators. Can you restore Tonga's rightful place amongst the great nations of the Pacific? Can you build a civilization that will stand the test of time?
